name: Acid reflux and GORD
overview: Acid reflux is when stomach acid flows back up into the food pipe, causing heartburn. It is very common and can often be eased with lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines. When it happens often, it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
symptoms: Heartburn: a burning feeling in the middle of the chest
An unpleasant sour taste in the mouth from stomach acid
Cough or hiccups that keep coming back
causes: Weakness of the muscle ring at the bottom of the food pipe
Certain foods and drinks such as coffee, alcohol, spicy or fatty foods
Some medicines, such as anti-inflammatory painkillers
A hiatus hernia
riskFactors: Large meals or eating late at night
diagnosis: Reflux is usually diagnosed from symptoms; tests such as an endoscopy may be used if symptoms are severe, persistent or there are warning signs.
treatment: Antacids and alginates from a pharmacy
Acid-reducing medicines prescribed by a doctor or bought from a pharmacy
Treatment for H. pylori infection if found
Surgery rarely, for severe cases
selfCare: Eat smaller, more frequent meals
Raise the head of your bed slightly
Avoid eating within 3 to 4 hours of bedtime
Lose weight if overweight, stop smoking, and cut down on trigger foods and alcohol
prevention: Avoid trigger foods and large late meals
whenToSeeDoctor: Heartburn most days for 3 weeks or more
Pharmacy medicines are not helping
Other symptoms such as food getting stuck, being sick or losing weight without trying
emergencySigns: Chest pain that spreads to the arm, jaw or back, or with breathlessness or sweating (could be a heart attack)
Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools
Difficulty swallowing that is getting worse quickly

name: Acne
overview: Acne is a common skin condition that causes spots, oily skin and sometimes skin that is hot or painful to touch. It most often affects teenagers but can continue into adulthood. Effective treatments are available.
symptoms: Red or darker spots (papules) and pus-filled spots
Large, painful lumps under the skin (nodules or cysts)
Mostly on the face, back and chest
causes: Hair follicles becoming blocked by oil and dead skin cells
Hormonal changes, especially during puberty
Bacteria in blocked follicles causing inflammation
riskFactors: Hormonal changes such as periods, pregnancy or PCOS
diagnosis: A GP or pharmacist diagnoses acne by looking at the skin.
treatment: Pharmacy creams and gels for mild acne
Prescription creams, antibiotic tablets or hormonal contraceptives
Specialist treatment for severe acne, prescribed by a dermatologist
selfCare: Wash the affected area gently twice a day
Do not squeeze or pick spots
Use non-oily (non-comedogenic) products
Be patient: treatments can take weeks to work
prevention: Start treatment early to reduce scarring
whenToSeeDoctor: Pharmacy treatments have not worked
Acne is moderate or severe, painful, or causing scarring
Acne is affecting your mood or confidence

name: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD)
overview: Age-related macular degeneration affects the middle part of your vision. It usually affects people over 50 and does not cause total blindness, but it can make everyday activities like reading and recognising faces difficult. Wet AMD can be treated if found early.
causes: Damage to the macula, part of the retina, with ageing
Dry AMD develops slowly; wet AMD is caused by abnormal blood vessels and can develop quickly
diagnosis: AMD is diagnosed during an eye examination, usually with a scan of the back of the eye (OCT).
treatment: Injections into the eye for wet AMD
No treatment yet to reverse dry AMD; support and low-vision aids help
Light therapy in some cases
selfCare: Stop smoking
Eat a healthy diet with leafy greens
Use magnifiers and good lighting
Regular eye tests
whenToSeeDoctor: Gradual changes in central vision
Difficulty reading or seeing fine detail
emergencySigns: Sudden distortion of vision or straight lines appearing wavy (get seen urgently by an eye specialist)
Sudden loss of vision

name: Alzheimer's disease
overview: Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. It gradually damages brain cells, affecting memory, thinking and behaviour. There is no cure, but treatments and support can help people live as well as possible.
causes: Build-up of abnormal proteins in the brain that damage nerve cells
A combination of age, genes, lifestyle and environment
riskFactors: Cardiovascular risk factors such as high blood pressure, smoking and diabetes
diagnosis: It is diagnosed through memory and thinking tests, a medical history, blood tests to rule out other causes, and sometimes brain scans at a specialist clinic.
treatment: Medicines that can help some symptoms for a time
Activities and therapies to support memory and wellbeing
Treatment for related problems such as low mood or sleep problems
Care and support planning
selfCare: Keep a routine and use memory aids
Stay active and socially connected
Make the home safe
Make plans for future care while able
prevention: Healthy lifestyle: activity, not smoking, healthy diet
whenToSeeDoctor: Worsening memory problems
Family members notice changes in memory or behaviour
emergencySigns: Sudden confusion or a rapid change in behaviour
A fall with head injury
Signs of stroke

name: Anaphylaxis
overview: Anaphylaxis is a severe, life-threatening allergic reaction that happens very quickly. It is a medical emergency. Adrenaline is the main treatment and should be given straight away if available.
symptoms: Swelling of the throat and tongue
Difficulty breathing, wheezing or noisy breathing
Skin that feels cold to the touch or a rash
causes: Foods such as nuts, milk, fish, shellfish and eggs
Insect stings, such as wasp or bee stings
Some medicines, such as certain antibiotics
Latex
riskFactors: Known allergy to stings or medicines
diagnosis: Anaphylaxis is diagnosed from symptoms during the reaction; an allergy specialist then tests for the trigger.
treatment: Adrenaline injection straight away, using an auto-injector if available
Emergency hospital treatment
Referral to an allergy specialist afterwards
selfCare: Call emergency services immediately
Use an adrenaline auto-injector if available; a second dose may be given after 5 minutes if no improvement
Lie down with legs raised, or sit up if breathing is difficult
Carry two auto-injectors at all times if prescribed
prevention: Carry prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors and know how to use them
whenToSeeDoctor: After any severe allergic reaction, for referral to an allergy specialist
If you have had a reaction and have not been tested
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing or swallowing
Swelling of the throat or tongue
Feeling faint, dizzy or collapsing
Confusion or loss of consciousness

name: Appendicitis
overview: Appendicitis is a painful swelling of the appendix, a small pouch attached to the large intestine. It is a medical emergency that usually needs surgery to remove the appendix. Without treatment, the appendix can burst.
symptoms: Pain that starts in the middle of the tummy and moves to the lower right side
Pain that gets worse when coughing, walking or pressing on the area
causes: Often unclear
Thought to be caused by a blockage of the appendix, which then becomes infected
riskFactors: Most common between ages 10 and 20, but can happen at any age
diagnosis: A doctor examines the tummy and may use blood and urine tests and an ultrasound or CT scan.
treatment: Surgery to remove the appendix, usually by keyhole surgery
Antibiotics, sometimes before or after surgery
selfCare: Do not eat or drink if you suspect appendicitis, as you may need surgery
Avoid painkillers that may mask symptoms until seen, unless advised
prevention: There is no known way to prevent appendicitis
whenToSeeDoctor: Tummy pain that gets steadily worse, especially on the lower right side: get urgent help the same day
Tummy pain with fever, being sick or loss of appetite
A child with tummy pain who will not walk normally or eat
emergencySigns: Pain that suddenly spreads across the whole tummy
Tummy pain that is getting worse with high temperature
Feeling very unwell, with fast heartbeat or collapse

name: Asthma
overview: Asthma is a common long-term condition where the airways become inflamed and narrow, making it hard to breathe at times. It usually starts in childhood but can begin at any age. With the right treatment most people can control their symptoms well.
symptoms: Coughing, often worse at night or early morning
causes: Inflamed, sensitive airways that react to triggers
Triggers such as colds, allergies (pollen, dust mites, pets), smoke, exercise, cold air and air pollution
riskFactors: Family history of asthma or allergies
Low birth weight or premature birth
Work exposure to dusts or chemicals
diagnosis: Asthma is diagnosed from symptoms and breathing tests such as spirometry, peak flow monitoring or a FeNO test.
treatment: Inhalers: relievers to ease symptoms and preventers to reduce airway inflammation
Combination inhalers
Tablets or other medicines if inhalers alone do not control symptoms
A personal asthma action plan
selfCare: Use inhalers as prescribed and check your technique
Know and avoid your triggers where possible
Follow your asthma action plan
Do not smoke
prevention: Take preventer medicine regularly if prescribed
Get flu and other recommended vaccines
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child may have asthma
You need your reliever inhaler 3 or more times a week
Symptoms wake you at night
Your asthma is affecting daily life
emergencySigns: Reliever inhaler is not helping
Too breathless to speak, eat or sleep
Breathing getting faster and you cannot catch your breath
Lips or fingers turning blue or grey
Drowsiness or confusion

name: Athlete's foot
overview: Athlete's foot is a common fungal infection that affects the feet, especially between the toes. It is usually not serious and can be treated with pharmacy antifungal creams, sprays or powders.
symptoms: Itchy white patches between the toes
Red, sore and flaky patches on the feet (may be less visible on darker skin)
causes: Fungal infection that thrives in warm, damp places
Spread by walking barefoot in places like changing rooms or sharing towels
riskFactors: Diabetes or a weakened immune system
diagnosis: A pharmacist or GP diagnoses athlete's foot by looking at the skin; a skin sample is rarely needed.
treatment: Antifungal creams, sprays or powders from a pharmacy
Prescription treatment if pharmacy products do not work
selfCare: Dry feet carefully, especially between the toes
Use a separate towel for your feet
Wear clean cotton socks and change them daily
Keep using treatment for the recommended time after symptoms clear
prevention: Wear flip-flops in communal showers and changing rooms
Do not share towels, socks or shoes
whenToSeeDoctor: Pharmacy treatment has not worked after 2 weeks
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system
Foot is red, hot and swollen (possible cellulitis)

name: Atrial fibrillation
overview: Atrial fibrillation is a common heart rhythm problem that causes an irregular and often fast heartbeat. It raises the risk of stroke because blood clots can form in the heart. Treatment controls the heart rate or rhythm and lowers stroke risk.
symptoms: Tiredness and less able to exercise
causes: High blood pressure
Coronary heart disease, heart failure or heart valve problems
Overactive thyroid
Heavy alcohol use
Sometimes no clear cause
diagnosis: AF is diagnosed with an electrocardiogram (ECG), sometimes using a portable monitor worn for a day or longer.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines to reduce the risk of stroke
Medicines to control heart rate or rhythm
Cardioversion (a controlled electric shock) to reset the rhythm
Catheter ablation in some people
selfCare: Take medicines exactly as prescribed
Limit alcohol and caffeine if they trigger symptoms
Keep to a healthy weight and be active
Learn to check your pulse
whenToSeeDoctor: Your heartbeat feels irregular or very fast
Palpitations with dizziness or breathlessness
An irregular pulse found on a smartwatch or home check
emergencySigns: Chest pain
Severe breathlessness
Fainting or collapse
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems

name: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)
overview: ADHD is a condition that affects attention, activity levels and impulse control. Symptoms usually start in childhood and often continue into adulthood. Support, strategies and medicines can help people manage day-to-day life.
symptoms: Short attention span and being easily distracted
causes: Strong genetic component: it often runs in families
Differences in brain development and function
riskFactors: Premature birth or low birth weight
Exposure to alcohol, smoking or drugs during pregnancy
diagnosis: ADHD is diagnosed by a specialist such as a psychiatrist or paediatrician, based on a detailed assessment of symptoms over time and in different settings.
treatment: Medicines prescribed and monitored by a specialist
Parent training and education programmes
Talking therapies such as CBT
Support at school or work
selfCare: Use routines, lists and reminders
Break tasks into smaller steps
Regular exercise and sleep
Healthy, regular meals
prevention: There is no known way to prevent ADHD
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child may have ADHD
Symptoms are causing problems at school, work or in relationships
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Chest pain or fainting while taking ADHD medicine

name: Back pain
overview: Back pain, especially in the lower back, is very common. It usually gets better within a few weeks or months. Staying active is one of the most helpful things you can do.
symptoms: Aching or stiffness anywhere along the spine
Pain that may spread to the buttocks or legs
Pain that is worse when bending, lifting or sitting for long periods
causes: Often no specific cause (non-specific back pain)
Strains or sprains from lifting or twisting
Poor posture or long periods of sitting
Conditions such as a slipped disc, sciatica or osteoarthritis
diagnosis: A GP or physiotherapist diagnoses back pain through questions and an examination; scans are usually not needed unless there are warning signs.
treatment: Staying active and continuing normal activities
Painkillers such as anti-inflammatory medicines
Exercises and physiotherapy
Talking therapies for long-term pain
selfCare: Keep moving; avoid bed rest
Use heat packs
Do gentle back exercises and stretches
Return to normal activities gradually
prevention: Regular exercise such as walking, swimming or yoga
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain does not improve after a few weeks
Pain stops you doing daily activities
Pain is very bad or getting worse
You also have numbness, tingling or weakness
emergencySigns: Numbness around the genitals or bottom
Loss of bladder or bowel control, or unable to pee
Weakness or numbness in both legs
Back pain with high temperature, or after a serious fall or accident
Severe pain with chest pain

name: Benign prostate enlargement (BPH)
overview: Benign prostate enlargement is when the prostate gland gets bigger, which is common in men over 50. It is not cancer and does not raise the risk of prostate cancer, but it can affect how you pee.
symptoms: Needing to pee more often or urgently
Feeling that the bladder has not fully emptied
causes: Hormonal changes linked to ageing
The exact cause is not fully understood
diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms and may do a urine test, a blood test (PSA) and a rectal examination to check the prostate.
treatment: Lifestyle changes
Medicines to relax the prostate or shrink it
Surgery for more severe symptoms
selfCare: Drink less in the evening
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Empty your bladder twice in a row (double voiding)
Bladder training
prevention: There is no proven way to prevent it; a healthy lifestyle may help
whenToSeeDoctor: Any changes in how you pee
Symptoms affecting sleep or daily life
Blood in urine
emergencySigns: Unable to pee at all, with a painful, swollen tummy
Pee problems with high temperature and shivering

name: Bipolar disorder
overview: Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings, from periods of depression to periods of very high mood and energy (mania or hypomania). It is a long-term condition, but treatment helps most people manage it well.
symptoms: Periods of depression: low mood, lack of energy, hopelessness
Periods of mania: feeling very happy or irritable, full of energy and ideas
Talking quickly and needing little sleep
Taking risks or making unusual decisions, such as spending sprees
Sometimes seeing or hearing things others do not (psychosis)
causes: A mix of genetic and environmental factors
Episodes can be triggered by stress, sleep disruption or substance use
diagnosis: Bipolar disorder is diagnosed by a psychiatrist after assessing mood patterns, symptoms and history over time.
treatment: Mood-stabilising medicines prescribed by a specialist
Talking therapies
Learning to recognise early warning signs of an episode
Hospital care during severe episodes
selfCare: Keep a regular sleep routine
Track your mood
Avoid alcohol and drugs
Take medicines as prescribed even when well
prevention: Recognise and act on early warning signs
whenToSeeDoctor: Periods of very high or very low mood
Mood changes affecting work or relationships
Side effects of medicines
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Severe mania or psychosis putting you or others at risk

name: Bowel cancer
overview: Bowel cancer is cancer of the large bowel (colon) or back passage (rectum). It is one of the most common cancers. Screening can find it early or even prevent it by removing growths called polyps.
symptoms: Changes in your poo, such as looser poo, pooing more often or constipation
Blood in your poo or bleeding from the bottom
Needing to poo more or less often than usual
Tummy pain or a lump in the tummy
Losing weight without trying and tiredness
causes: Changes in bowel cells, often starting in non-cancerous growths called polyps
Influenced by age, genes, diet and lifestyle
riskFactors: Diet high in red and processed meat and low in fibre
diagnosis: Bowel cancer is diagnosed with a stool test (FIT), a colonoscopy with biopsy, and scans.
treatment: Surgery
Chemotherapy
Radiotherapy
Targeted medicines and immunotherapy
selfCare: Attend bowel screening when invited
Report changes in bowel habits
prevention: Eat plenty of fibre and less red and processed meat
Do not smoke and limit alcohol
whenToSeeDoctor: Changes in bowel habits lasting 3 weeks or more
Blood in your poo
Unexplained weight loss or tiredness
A lump in your tummy
emergencySigns: Heavy bleeding from the bottom
Unable to poo or pass wind with a swollen tummy and vomiting
Severe tummy pain

name: Breast cancer
overview: Breast cancer is one of the most common cancers. It mostly affects women but can also affect men. Finding it early through screening and checking your breasts improves the chance of successful treatment.
symptoms: A new lump or thickening in the breast or armpit
A change in the size or shape of a breast
Skin changes such as dimpling, puckering or redness
Changes to the nipple, such as turning inwards
Discharge or bleeding from the nipple
A rash on or around the nipple
causes: Changes in breast cells that make them grow uncontrollably
Influenced by age, genes, hormones and lifestyle
riskFactors: Family history or inherited gene changes such as BRCA1 or BRCA2
diagnosis: Breast cancer is diagnosed with a breast examination, a mammogram or ultrasound, and a biopsy.
treatment: Surgery
Radiotherapy
Chemotherapy
Hormone therapy and targeted medicines
selfCare: Get to know how your breasts normally look and feel
Attend screening when invited
whenToSeeDoctor: Any new lump or change in the breast or armpit
Nipple changes or discharge
Skin changes on the breast

name: Bronchiolitis
overview: Bronchiolitis is a common chest infection that affects babies and children under 2. It is usually mild and gets better within 2 to 3 weeks, but some babies need hospital care.
symptoms: Runny nose and cough at first
Feeding less and fewer wet nappies
causes: Viral infection, most commonly respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses bronchiolitis from the symptoms and by listening to the chest.
treatment: Most babies get better at home with fluids and rest
Hospital care for breathing or feeding problems, including oxygen and fluids
Antibiotics are not used because it is caused by a virus
selfCare: Give small feeds more often
Use saline drops to ease a blocked nose if advised
Keep your baby upright
Keep your baby away from smoke
prevention: Keep babies away from people with colds
RSV immunisation for babies or in pregnancy where offered
whenToSeeDoctor: Your baby is feeding much less than usual
Fewer wet nappies
A high temperature
Your baby seems very tired or irritable
emergencySigns: Pauses in breathing
Struggling to breathe, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
Lips or tongue turning blue or grey
Your baby is floppy or not responding

name: Bronchitis
overview: Bronchitis is an infection of the main airways of the lungs that causes a cough. It usually follows a cold and gets better on its own within about 3 weeks. Antibiotics are not usually needed.
symptoms: Cough that may bring up clear, yellow, grey or green mucus
causes: Usually a viral infection, often the same viruses that cause colds and flu
Less often a bacterial infection
Smoke and other irritants can make it more likely
diagnosis: A GP usually diagnoses bronchitis by asking about symptoms and listening to the chest; a chest X-ray may be used to rule out pneumonia.
treatment: Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen
Antibiotics only if a bacterial infection is suspected or there is a higher risk of complications
Pharmacy cough remedies, following pharmacist advice
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Honey and lemon in warm water (not for babies under 1)
Avoid smoking and smoky places
prevention: Get the flu vaccine if eligible
whenToSeeDoctor: Cough is very bad or lasts longer than 3 weeks
High temperature for more than 3 days
Coughing up blood-streaked mucus
You have a long-term heart or lung condition
Breathlessness or chest pain
emergencySigns: Severe difficulty breathing
Coughing up a lot of blood
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Sudden confusion

name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
overview: Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes tingling, numbness and pain in the hand and fingers. It is common and often gets better with simple treatments.
symptoms: Tingling or pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle fingers
Numbness or pain in the hand and fingers
causes: Pressure on the median nerve as it passes through a narrow channel in the wrist (the carpal tunnel)
Swelling in the wrist, for example from repetitive use, pregnancy, injury or arthritis
riskFactors: Diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis or an underactive thyroid
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses carpal tunnel syndrome from symptoms and an examination; nerve conduction tests may be used.
treatment: Wrist splints, especially at night
Painkillers
Steroid injections
Surgery to release pressure on the nerve if symptoms persist
selfCare: Wear a wrist splint at night
Take breaks from repetitive tasks
Hand exercises
prevention: Take regular breaks from repetitive hand movements
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms not improving after a few weeks
Symptoms affecting sleep or daily activities
Constant numbness or weakness in the hand
emergencySigns: Sudden numbness or weakness in one arm or hand with face drooping or speech problems (possible stroke)

name: Cataracts
overview: Cataracts are when the lens inside the eye becomes cloudy, causing blurred or misty vision. They are very common in older people. Surgery to replace the cloudy lens is safe and effective.
symptoms: Finding lights too bright or glaring
causes: Natural changes in the lens with age
Diabetes, eye injury, long-term steroid use, or sun exposure
diagnosis: Cataracts are diagnosed during an eye test by an optometrist or eye specialist.
treatment: Stronger glasses and brighter lighting in early stages
Surgery to replace the cloudy lens with an artificial one
selfCare: Use brighter lights at home
Wear sunglasses
Have regular eye tests
whenToSeeDoctor: Vision is becoming blurry or cloudy
Vision problems affecting daily life such as reading or driving
emergencySigns: Sudden loss of vision
Severe eye pain or redness after cataract surgery

name: Cellulitis
overview: Cellulitis is an infection of the deeper layers of the skin and the tissue beneath it. It can be serious if not treated quickly, but usually responds well to antibiotics.
symptoms: Skin that is red, hot, swollen and painful (redness may be harder to see on darker skin)
Feeling generally unwell, with high temperature or shivering
causes: Bacteria, most often streptococcus or staphylococcus, entering through broken skin
Entry points such as cuts, grazes, bites, ulcers or cracked skin from athlete's foot or eczema
riskFactors: Skin conditions such as eczema or athlete's foot
Diabetes or a weakened immune system
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses cellulitis by examining the skin; blood tests or swabs may be done if it is severe.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor
Painkillers
Hospital treatment with antibiotics through a drip if severe
selfCare: Raise the affected area to reduce swelling
Drink plenty of fluids
Finish the course of antibiotics
Avoid compression stockings until healed unless advised otherwise
prevention: Clean and cover cuts and grazes
Treat skin conditions such as athlete's foot or eczema
Keep skin moisturised to prevent cracking
whenToSeeDoctor: Skin is red, hot, swollen and painful
Symptoms not improving 2 to 3 days after starting antibiotics
emergencySigns: Skin around the eye or face is red, swollen and painful
Fast heartbeat or fast breathing
Confusion or feeling faint
Cold, clammy, pale or blotchy skin
Rapidly spreading redness with feeling very unwell

name: Cervical cancer
overview: Cervical cancer develops in the cervix, the entrance to the womb from the vagina. Almost all cases are caused by long-lasting infection with high-risk types of HPV. HPV vaccination and cervical screening can prevent most cases.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in early stages
Vaginal bleeding that is unusual, such as after sex, between periods or after menopause
Pain in the lower back or pelvis
causes: Persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV)
Abnormal cell changes in the cervix that develop over years
riskFactors: A weakened immune system, such as with HIV
diagnosis: Cervical cancer is diagnosed through screening (HPV test), a colposcopy to look at the cervix, and a biopsy.
treatment: Surgery
Radiotherapy
Chemotherapy
Treatment of abnormal cells before they become cancer
selfCare: Attend cervical screening when invited
Report unusual bleeding promptly
whenToSeeDoctor: Bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause
Unusual vaginal discharge
Pain during sex
emergencySigns: Heavy vaginal bleeding that will not stop

name: Chickenpox
overview: Chickenpox is a common illness that mainly affects children and causes an itchy, spotty rash. It is usually mild and gets better on its own within 1 to 2 weeks, but it can be more serious for adults, pregnant people, newborns and people with weakened immunity.
symptoms: Itchy spots that appear anywhere on the body
Spots that fill with fluid to become blisters, then scab over
causes: Infection with the varicella-zoster virus
Spread by close contact and through the air from coughs and sneezes
Contact with fluid from the blisters
riskFactors: Never having had chickenpox or the vaccine
Contact with someone with chickenpox or shingles
diagnosis: Chickenpox is usually recognised from the typical rash; tests are rarely needed.
treatment: Paracetamol for pain and fever
Cooling creams or gels and antihistamines for itching, as advised by a pharmacist
Antiviral medicine for some higher-risk people, prescribed by a doctor
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids
Keep nails short and cover hands at night to reduce scratching
Wear loose, cotton clothing
Stay away from school or work until all spots have crusted over
prevention: Keep away from pregnant people, newborns and people with weak immunity while infectious
whenToSeeDoctor: Skin around blisters becomes red, hot or painful
You are pregnant, or have a weakened immune system, and have been exposed or have symptoms
A baby under 4 weeks has chickenpox
An adult has chickenpox
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing
Chest pain
A stiff neck, severe headache or sensitivity to light
Confusion, seizures or being very drowsy
A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it

name: Chlamydia
overview: Chlamydia is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. Most people have no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know. It is easily treated with antibiotics, but untreated it can cause long-term problems such as infertility.
symptoms: Unusual discharge from the vagina, penis or bottom
Pain in the tummy, bleeding after sex or between periods
Pain and swelling in the testicles
causes: Chlamydia trachomatis bacteria passed on through unprotected vaginal, anal or oral sex
Sharing sex toys
From mother to baby during birth
riskFactors: A new sexual partner or multiple partners
diagnosis: Chlamydia is diagnosed with a urine test or a swab, available at sexual health clinics, GPs and via home testing kits.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor or nurse
Avoid sex until you and your partner(s) have finished treatment
Partners should be tested and treated
selfCare: Finish the full course of antibiotics
Tell recent sexual partners so they can get tested
prevention: Regular STI testing, especially with new partners
whenToSeeDoctor: You have symptoms of an STI
A partner has an STI
You have had sex without a condom with a new partner
emergencySigns: Severe tummy pain with fever
Severe pain in one side of the lower tummy with a missed period (possible ectopic pregnancy)

name: Chronic kidney disease (CKD)
overview: Chronic kidney disease is a long-term condition where the kidneys do not work as well as they should. It is common, especially in older people, and often causes no symptoms in the early stages. Treatment can slow it down and lower the risk of heart disease.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms in early stages
Blood in urine or needing to pee more at night
causes: High blood pressure
Diabetes
High cholesterol
Kidney infections, inflammation or inherited kidney conditions
Long-term use of some medicines such as anti-inflammatory painkillers
riskFactors: Being of South Asian, African or African-Caribbean descent
diagnosis: CKD is diagnosed with blood tests (to estimate kidney function) and urine tests, often found during routine checks for people at risk.
treatment: Controlling blood pressure and blood sugar
Medicines to protect the kidneys and heart
Dialysis or kidney transplant for kidney failure
selfCare: Stop smoking
Healthy diet with less salt
Be physically active
Limit alcohol
Check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking new medicines
whenToSeeDoctor: You have diabetes or high blood pressure and have not had kidney checks
Persistent symptoms such as swollen ankles or tiredness
Blood in urine
emergencySigns: Severe shortness of breath
Passing very little or no urine
Chest pain or confusion

name: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
overview: COPD is a long-term lung condition, including emphysema and chronic bronchitis, that makes it harder to breathe. It is mostly caused by smoking and gets slowly worse over time. Treatment and stopping smoking can slow it down and help people stay active.
causes: Smoking, the main cause
Long-term exposure to fumes, dust or air pollution
Rarely, an inherited condition called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
riskFactors: Indoor smoke from cooking or heating fuels
diagnosis: COPD is diagnosed with a breathing test called spirometry, along with a chest X-ray and blood tests to rule out other causes.
treatment: Stopping smoking
Inhalers to open the airways
Pulmonary rehabilitation (an exercise and education programme)
Tablets, oxygen therapy or surgery in some cases
selfCare: Stop smoking
Stay as active as possible
Use inhalers correctly
Have a rescue plan for flare-ups
prevention: Avoid workplace dust and fumes with proper protection
Flu, pneumococcal and other recommended vaccines
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent breathlessness, cough or wheeze
Frequent chest infections
Symptoms getting worse over days (a flare-up)
emergencySigns: Severe breathlessness that is not relieved by usual treatment
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Confusion or drowsiness
Chest pain

name: Coeliac disease
overview: Coeliac disease is a lifelong condition where the immune system attacks the body's own tissues when gluten is eaten. This damages the lining of the gut. A strict gluten-free diet controls the condition.
symptoms: Unexplained weight loss or poor growth in children
causes: An autoimmune reaction to gluten, a protein in wheat, barley and rye
Genes play a part: it is more common in people with a close relative who has it
riskFactors: Close family member with coeliac disease
Type 1 diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease
diagnosis: Coeliac disease is diagnosed with a blood test followed by a biopsy of the small bowel; you must keep eating gluten until testing is complete.
treatment: A lifelong strict gluten-free diet
Support from a dietitian
Supplements if you have low iron, vitamin or mineral levels
selfCare: Read food labels carefully
Avoid cross-contamination with gluten when preparing food
Attend regular check-ups
prevention: There is no known way to prevent coeliac disease; testing family members can find it early
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent diarrhoea, bloating or tummy pain
Unexplained tiredness, weight loss or anaemia
A close relative has coeliac disease

name: Common cold
overview: A common cold is a mild viral infection of the nose and throat. It usually gets better on its own within about 1 to 2 weeks. Antibiotics do not work against colds because they are caused by viruses.
symptoms: Feeling generally unwell or slightly raised temperature
causes: Infection with one of many cold viruses, most often rhinoviruses
Spread through droplets from coughs and sneezes
Touching contaminated surfaces and then the eyes, nose or mouth
riskFactors: Close contact with people who have a cold
Young children and those around them, such as in nurseries and schools
diagnosis: A cold is usually recognised from the symptoms and does not normally need a doctor or any tests.
treatment: Rest and plenty of fluids
Paracetamol or ibuprofen to ease aches and fever
Pharmacy remedies such as decongestants, following the label and pharmacist advice
selfCare: Rest and sleep
Drink plenty of water
Gargle with salt water for a sore throat
Use honey and lemon in a warm drink (not for babies under 1)
prevention: Wash hands often with soap and warm water
Use tissues for coughs and sneezes and bin them straight away
Avoid sharing towels and cups with someone who is ill
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms have not improved after 3 weeks
Symptoms get suddenly worse
A high temperature or feeling hot and shivery
You have a long-term condition or weakened immune system and are concerned
Chest pain or coughing up blood-stained mucus
emergencySigns: Severe difficulty breathing
Lips or tongue turning blue or grey
Confusion or being very difficult to wake

name: Conjunctivitis
overview: Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the thin layer covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids. It is common and often gets better on its own within about 2 weeks. It can be caused by infection or allergy.
symptoms: Discharge that may stick the eyelashes together
causes: Viral infection
Bacterial infection
Allergies such as pollen or dust
Irritants such as chlorine or smoke
riskFactors: Close contact with someone who has infectious conjunctivitis
diagnosis: A pharmacist or GP can usually tell from looking at the eye and asking about symptoms; swabs are rarely needed.
treatment: Often clears without treatment
Antibiotic eye drops or ointment if a bacterial infection is likely
Antihistamine eye drops or tablets for allergic conjunctivitis
selfCare: Clean eyelids with cotton wool soaked in cooled boiled water
Use a cool compress
Stop wearing contact lenses until eyes are better
Do not rub the eyes
prevention: Do not share towels, pillows or eye make-up
whenToSeeDoctor: A baby under 28 days old has red, sticky eyes
Symptoms have not improved after 2 weeks
You wear contact lenses and have symptoms
emergencySigns: Changes in vision such as blurred vision or wavy lines
Sensitivity to light that is painful
Very red, painful eye
Severe headache with nausea

name: Constipation
overview: Constipation means pooing less often than usual or finding it hard to poo. It is common at all ages and can usually be eased with changes to diet and lifestyle.
symptoms: Pooing fewer than 3 times a week
Poo that is large, dry, hard or lumpy
Feeling that you have not fully emptied your bowels
causes: Not eating enough fibre
Not drinking enough fluids
Not moving enough
Ignoring the urge to poo
Some medicines, such as certain painkillers
Pregnancy or conditions such as IBS or an underactive thyroid
diagnosis: Constipation is usually recognised from symptoms; a GP may examine you or arrange tests if it is persistent or there are warning signs.
treatment: Diet and lifestyle changes
Laxatives from a pharmacy or prescribed by a doctor
Treating any underlying cause
selfCare: Eat more fibre such as fruit, vegetables and wholegrains
Drink plenty of water
Exercise more
Do not delay going to the toilet; raising feet on a stool may help
whenToSeeDoctor: Constipation is not improving with treatment
You are often constipated or bloated
Blood in your poo
Unexplained weight loss or tiredness
A baby or child is constipated and it is not getting better
emergencySigns: Unable to poo or pass wind with a swollen tummy and vomiting
Severe tummy pain
Bleeding heavily from the bottom

name: Coronary heart disease
overview: Coronary heart disease happens when the arteries supplying the heart become narrowed by fatty deposits. It can cause chest pain (angina) and heart attacks. It cannot be cured, but treatment and lifestyle changes can greatly reduce the risk.
symptoms: Chest pain or tightness (angina), often brought on by exertion or stress
Pain in the arm, neck, jaw, back or stomach
Some people have no symptoms before a heart attack
causes: Build-up of fatty material in the walls of the coronary arteries (atherosclerosis)
Damage to arteries from smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes
diagnosis: Doctors use a risk assessment, blood tests, an ECG, and tests such as an exercise test, CT scan or coronary angiogram.
treatment: Medicines to reduce symptoms and risk of heart attack, prescribed by a doctor
Procedures to widen arteries (angioplasty and stents)
Coronary artery bypass surgery
Cardiac rehabilitation
selfCare: Stop smoking
Eat a healthy diet and be physically active
Keep blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes under control
Carry any prescribed angina spray and know how to use it
prevention: Managing blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Chest pain or tightness that comes on with activity and settles with rest
Increasing breathlessness
Angina that is happening more often or with less effort
emergencySigns: Chest pain that is sudden, severe or lasts more than a few minutes, or does not settle with rest or your angina medicine
Chest pain spreading to the arms, neck, jaw or back
Chest pain with sweating, breathlessness or feeling sick

name: COVID-19
overview: COVID-19 is an infection caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus. Most people have a mild illness and recover at home, but some people become seriously ill. Vaccination lowers the risk of severe illness.
symptoms: Loss or change to sense of smell or taste
Sore throat, blocked or runny nose
causes: Infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus
Spread through droplets and tiny airborne particles from infected people
Less often, touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as heart, lung or kidney disease or diabetes
diagnosis: COVID-19 is confirmed with a rapid lateral flow test or a laboratory PCR test from a nose or throat swab.
treatment: Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for most people
Antiviral or other treatments for people at highest risk, prescribed by a doctor
Hospital care, including oxygen, for severe illness
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Try to stay at home and avoid contact with others while unwell or with a high temperature
Ventilate rooms by opening windows
prevention: Wash hands regularly and cover coughs and sneezes
Let fresh air into shared spaces
whenToSeeDoctor: You are worried about your symptoms or a child's symptoms
Symptoms are getting worse or not improving
You are at higher risk and test positive, in case treatment is suitable
Symptoms last 4 weeks or more
emergencySigns: Severe shortness of breath or breathing getting worse quickly
Being unable to complete short sentences when at rest
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Confusion or being very drowsy
Persistent chest pain or pressure

name: Crohn's disease
overview: Crohn's disease is a lifelong condition where parts of the digestive system become inflamed. It is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. Symptoms come and go in flare-ups, and treatment aims to control inflammation and keep it in remission.
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Thought to involve genes, the immune system and gut bacteria
Smoking increases the risk and makes it worse
riskFactors: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease
Often starts between the teens and 30s
diagnosis: Crohn's disease is diagnosed with blood and stool tests, a colonoscopy with biopsies, and sometimes scans.
treatment: Medicines to reduce inflammation, such as steroids
Immunosuppressant and biological medicines to keep it under control
Surgery to remove damaged parts of the bowel in some cases
Dietary support
selfCare: Stop smoking
Keep a symptom diary to spot triggers
Eat a balanced diet with dietitian advice
Attend regular check-ups
whenToSeeDoctor: Blood in your poo
Diarrhoea for more than 7 days
Frequent tummy pain or unexplained weight loss
Signs of a flare-up if you already have Crohn's
emergencySigns: Severe tummy pain
Vomiting and unable to keep fluids down
Heavy bleeding from the bottom
High fever with tummy pain

name: Croup
overview: Croup is a common childhood condition that affects the windpipe and airways, causing a distinctive barking cough. It is usually mild and gets better within 48 hours, but can sometimes make breathing difficult.
symptoms: A barking cough, often worse at night
A rasping sound when breathing in (stridor)
Cold-like symptoms such as a runny nose and high temperature
causes: Usually a viral infection, such as parainfluenza virus
Spread through coughs and sneezes
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses croup from the typical cough and by examining the child's breathing.
treatment: Steroid medicine prescribed by a doctor to reduce swelling in the airways
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever or discomfort
Hospital treatment, including oxygen, for severe croup
selfCare: Keep your child calm and comfortable; crying can make it worse
Give plenty of fluids
Sit your child upright
Do not put a child in a steamy room or give them steam to breathe
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has croup
Symptoms are getting worse or lasting more than 48 hours
Your child has a high temperature or seems unwell
emergencySigns: Struggling to breathe, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
Unusually drowsy or floppy
Drooling or unable to swallow
Making a high-pitched noise when breathing at rest

name: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)
overview: A DVT is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg. It can be serious because part of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism). It is treated with medicines that stop clots growing.
symptoms: Throbbing or cramping pain in one leg, usually the calf or thigh
Warm skin around the painful area
Red or darker skin around the painful area
Swollen, hard veins that are sore to touch
causes: Slow or reduced blood flow in the deep veins, for example during long periods of immobility
Damage to a vein wall, such as from surgery or injury
Blood that clots more easily than usual, due to pregnancy, hormones, cancer or inherited conditions
riskFactors: Being immobile, such as after surgery, in hospital or on long journeys
Combined contraceptive pill or hormone therapy
diagnosis: A DVT is diagnosed with a blood test (D-dimer) and an ultrasound scan of the leg.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines to stop the clot growing
Compression stockings may be advised for symptoms
Occasionally procedures to remove the clot
selfCare: Take anticoagulants exactly as prescribed
Keep active and walk regularly
Raise the leg when resting
prevention: Keep moving during long journeys and after surgery
Drink fluids and avoid long periods of sitting
Follow hospital advice on clot prevention
Stop smoking and keep to a healthy weight
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain and swelling in one leg (get help urgently, the same day)
Symptoms in a leg after surgery, a long journey or during pregnancy
emergencySigns: Sudden breathlessness
Chest pain, especially when breathing in
Coughing up blood
Fast heartbeat or collapse

name: Dementia
overview: Dementia is a group of symptoms caused by diseases that damage the brain, affecting memory, thinking and daily life. It is not a normal part of ageing. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause, followed by vascular dementia.
symptoms: Memory loss, especially of recent events
causes: Alzheimer's disease
Vascular dementia from reduced blood flow to the brain
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Frontotemporal dementia
riskFactors: High blood pressure, diabetes and smoking
diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms, does memory tests and blood tests, and may refer to a memory clinic for specialist assessment and brain scans.
treatment: Medicines that may help some symptoms of Alzheimer's or Lewy body dementia
Managing risk factors in vascular dementia
Cognitive stimulation and other activities
Support for carers and planning for the future
selfCare: Keep active, physically and socially
Use reminders such as calendars and lists
Keep a regular routine
Plan ahead, including legal and financial matters
prevention: Do not smoke and limit alcohol
whenToSeeDoctor: Memory problems that are getting worse
Concern from family or friends about memory or behaviour
Difficulty managing daily tasks
emergencySigns: Sudden confusion or rapid worsening (could be infection, stroke or delirium)
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems

name: Dengue
overview: Dengue is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes in tropical and subtropical regions. Many people have no or mild symptoms, but a small number develop severe dengue, which needs urgent hospital care.
symptoms: Severe headache and pain behind the eyes
causes: Dengue virus passed on by bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, which bite mainly during the day
The same mosquitoes can spread other infections such as Zika and chikungunya, which can cause similar symptoms
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to tropical and subtropical areas
Previous dengue infection (raises the risk of severe dengue with a second infection)
diagnosis: Dengue is diagnosed with blood tests, alongside your symptoms and travel history.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment; care focuses on rest, fluids and paracetamol for pain and fever
Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers, which can increase bleeding risk
Hospital care for severe dengue
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use paracetamol rather than anti-inflammatory painkillers
Watch closely for warning signs as the fever goes down
prevention: Use insect repellent and cover up, especially during the day
Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed
Vaccination for some people, depending on country and past infection
whenToSeeDoctor: Fever during or after travel to an area with dengue
Symptoms not improving after a few days
emergencySigns: Severe stomach pain
Persistent vomiting
Bleeding gums or nose, or blood in vomit or stool
Fast breathing
Restlessness, extreme tiredness or cold clammy skin

name: Depression
overview: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days. It is a common mental health condition where low mood or loss of interest lasts for weeks or months and affects daily life. It is treatable, and most people recover with the right support.
symptoms: Loss of interest or enjoyment in things
Difficulty concentrating, or thoughts of self-harm or suicide
causes: Often a mix of factors rather than one cause
Stressful life events such as bereavement, divorce, job loss or illness
Family history and personality
Long-term health conditions, alcohol or drug use
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses depression by talking about symptoms, how long they have lasted and how they affect daily life.
treatment: Talking therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)
Antidepressant medicines prescribed by a doctor
Combination of therapy and medicine
Specialist mental health care for severe depression
selfCare: Stay connected with people you trust
Be physically active
Keep a regular sleep routine
Avoid alcohol and drugs
Use self-help and peer support
prevention: Seeking help early when mood is low
whenToSeeDoctor: Low mood or loss of interest lasting more than 2 weeks
Depression affecting work, relationships or daily life
Treatment is not helping
emergencySigns: Thoughts of ending your life or making plans to do so
Having harmed yourself seriously
Feeling unable to keep yourself safe

name: Diverticular disease and diverticulitis
overview: Diverticula are small bulges or pockets in the lining of the large intestine, which are common with age. When they cause symptoms it is called diverticular disease, and when they become inflamed or infected it is called diverticulitis.
symptoms: Tummy pain, usually in the lower left side, that may come and go
With diverticulitis: constant, severe pain, high temperature and feeling sick
causes: Weak spots in the bowel wall that bulge out under pressure
Linked to a low-fibre diet and ageing
riskFactors: Some medicines such as anti-inflammatory painkillers
diagnosis: It is diagnosed from symptoms, blood tests and sometimes a CT scan or colonoscopy.
treatment: High-fibre diet and painkillers such as paracetamol for diverticular disease
Antibiotics may be used for diverticulitis
Hospital treatment or surgery for complications
selfCare: Eat a high-fibre diet and increase fibre gradually
Drink plenty of fluids
Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers unless advised
whenToSeeDoctor: Lower tummy pain that comes and goes
Changes in bowel habit
Blood in your poo
emergencySigns: Severe or constant tummy pain with high temperature
Heavy bleeding from the bottom
Vomiting and unable to keep fluids down

name: Ear infection
overview: Ear infections are very common, especially in young children. Most get better on their own within about 3 days. They can affect the middle ear behind the eardrum or the outer ear canal.
symptoms: Being sick or lack of energy
Discharge running out of the ear
Itching or irritation in the ear
causes: Viral or bacterial infection, often after a cold
Water trapped in the ear canal (outer ear infection)
Damage to the skin of the ear canal
riskFactors: Using cotton buds in the ears
diagnosis: A GP looks inside the ear with an otoscope to check the eardrum and ear canal.
treatment: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever
Antibiotics are not usually needed but may be prescribed in some cases
Ear drops for outer ear infections, prescribed by a doctor or recommended by a pharmacist
selfCare: Hold a warm or cold flannel on the ear
Do not put anything inside the ear, such as cotton buds
Keep the ear dry
prevention: Keep up to date with routine childhood vaccines
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms last more than 3 days
Swelling around the ear
Fluid coming out of the ear
Hearing loss or a change in hearing
Frequent ear infections
A child under 2 has an infection in both ears
emergencySigns: Severe headache with a stiff neck
Sudden swelling, redness or pain behind the ear
Confusion, drowsiness or a seizure

name: Eczema (atopic eczema)
overview: Atopic eczema is a common long-term condition that makes the skin itchy, dry and cracked. It often starts in childhood and may improve with age. There is no cure, but treatments and good skin care can control it.
symptoms: Itchy, dry, cracked or sore skin
Patches that may look red on lighter skin or darker brown, purple or grey on darker skin
Commonly on the hands, inside the elbows, behind the knees, and on the face and scalp in children
causes: A mix of genes and a skin barrier that loses moisture easily
Flare-ups triggered by soaps, detergents, stress, weather changes, infections or allergens
riskFactors: Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses eczema by looking at the skin and asking about symptoms and family history.
treatment: Emollients (moisturisers) used every day
Topical steroid creams for flare-ups
Other creams or tablets prescribed by a doctor or dermatologist for severe eczema
Antibiotics if the skin becomes infected
selfCare: Use emollients often, including instead of soap
Avoid triggers such as perfumed products
Keep nails short and avoid scratching
Wear soft cotton clothing
prevention: Regular emollient use to reduce flare-ups
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child has eczema
Eczema is not improving with treatment
Skin looks infected: weeping, crusting or painful
emergencySigns: Painful eczema that is getting worse quickly, with fluid-filled blisters and feeling unwell or feverish (possible eczema herpeticum)

name: Endometriosis
overview: Endometriosis is a long-term condition where tissue similar to the lining of the womb grows in other places, such as the ovaries and fallopian tubes. It can cause painful periods and pelvic pain, and can affect fertility. Treatments can help manage symptoms.
symptoms: Period pain that stops you doing normal activities
Pain in the lower tummy or back (pelvic pain)
Pain when pooing or peeing during a period
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Possible factors include genetics, immune system problems and menstrual blood flowing backwards into the pelvis
riskFactors: Starting periods at a young age
diagnosis: Endometriosis can be suspected from symptoms and scans, but is often confirmed by keyhole surgery (laparoscopy).
treatment: Painkillers
Hormone treatments such as the contraceptive pill or other hormonal medicines
Surgery to remove endometriosis tissue
Fertility treatment if needed
selfCare: Use heat pads or warm baths for pain
Keep a symptom diary
Gentle exercise
Join a support group
prevention: There is no known way to prevent endometriosis
whenToSeeDoctor: Period pain that affects daily life
Pain during sex
Difficulty getting pregnant
Symptoms not improving with treatment
emergencySigns: Sudden, severe pelvic pain with fainting or feeling very unwell

name: Epilepsy
overview: Epilepsy is a condition where sudden bursts of electrical activity in the brain cause repeated seizures. It can start at any age. Most people can control their seizures with medicine.
symptoms: Strange sensations such as tingling, a rising feeling in the tummy or unusual smells
causes: Often no clear cause is found
Brain damage from stroke, head injury, infection such as meningitis, or a tumour
Genetic factors
riskFactors: Previous serious head injury or stroke
diagnosis: Epilepsy is diagnosed by a specialist using a description of the seizures, an EEG to record brain activity, and brain scans such as MRI.
treatment: Anti-seizure medicines
Surgery for some people
Special diets or nerve-stimulation devices in some cases
selfCare: Take medicines regularly as prescribed
Get enough sleep and avoid known triggers such as alcohol excess
Follow safety advice for bathing, swimming and driving
Share a seizure action plan with family and friends
prevention: Prevent head injuries, for example by wearing helmets
Take medicines regularly to reduce seizures
whenToSeeDoctor: Someone has a seizure for the first time
Seizures become more frequent or change
Side effects from medicines
You are planning pregnancy
emergencySigns: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Repeated seizures without recovering in between
First-ever seizure
Serious injury or breathing difficulty during a seizure
Seizure in water

name: Erectile dysfunction
overview: Erectile dysfunction is when you cannot get or keep an erection. It is very common, especially with age, and can be a sign of other health problems such as heart disease or diabetes. Effective treatments are available.
symptoms: Difficulty keeping an erection during sex
Reduced sexual desire in some cases
causes: Physical causes such as narrowed blood vessels, high blood pressure, diabetes or hormone problems
Psychological causes such as stress, anxiety or depression
Alcohol, smoking or some medicines
riskFactors: Heart disease, diabetes or high blood pressure
diagnosis: A GP or sexual health clinic asks about symptoms and may check blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and hormone levels.
treatment: Medicines that increase blood flow to the penis, prescribed by a doctor or pharmacist
Treating underlying conditions
Counselling or sex therapy
Vacuum pumps or other devices
selfCare: Stop smoking
Limit alcohol
Keep to a healthy weight
Exercise regularly
Manage stress
prevention: Control blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Erection problems that keep happening
You have other symptoms such as chest pain or breathlessness on exertion
emergencySigns: An erection lasting more than 4 hours (priapism)
Chest pain during sexual activity

name: Febrile seizures
overview: Febrile seizures are fits that can happen when a child has a high temperature. They are frightening to see but are usually harmless and most children recover fully. They are most common between 6 months and 3 years.
symptoms: Body becoming stiff and arms and legs twitching
Sleepiness for up to an hour afterwards
causes: A rapid rise in temperature during an infection such as a cold, flu, ear infection or chickenpox
Rarely, after some vaccinations
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses a febrile seizure from the description and checks for the cause of the fever.
treatment: Most stop on their own without treatment
Treatment of the underlying infection
Hospital care for long or repeated seizures
selfCare: During a seizure, place your child on their side on a soft surface
Do not put anything in their mouth
Time the seizure
Stay with your child
prevention: There is no reliable way to prevent febrile seizures; fever medicines make children more comfortable but do not prevent seizures
whenToSeeDoctor: After any first febrile seizure, even if it stopped
Your child seems unwell after a seizure
emergencySigns: A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
First-ever seizure
Difficulty breathing or not waking up afterwards
Another seizure soon after the first
Signs of meningitis such as a rash that does not fade or a stiff neck

name: Flu (influenza)
overview: Flu is a viral infection of the nose, throat and lungs that tends to come on quickly. Most people feel better within about a week, but it can be serious for older people, pregnant people, young children and those with long-term conditions. A yearly vaccine is the best protection.
symptoms: Loss of appetite, diarrhoea or tummy pain
causes: Infection with influenza viruses
Spread by droplets from coughs and sneezes
Touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as heart disease, lung disease or diabetes
diagnosis: Flu is usually diagnosed from symptoms during flu season; a swab test may be used in some settings, especially for people at higher risk.
treatment: Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and aches
Antiviral medicines may be prescribed for people at higher risk of complications
Antibiotics only if a bacterial complication develops
selfCare: Rest and keep warm
Drink plenty of fluids
Stay away from others while you have a high temperature
prevention: Catch coughs and sneezes in a tissue
whenToSeeDoctor: You are worried about a baby's or child's symptoms
You are 65 or over, pregnant, or have a long-term condition or weakened immune system
Symptoms have not improved after 7 days
Symptoms get worse after starting to improve
emergencySigns: Sudden chest pain
Difficulty breathing
Coughing up a lot of blood
Confusion, seizures or being hard to wake
Lips or skin turning blue or grey

name: Food allergy
overview: A food allergy is when the immune system reacts to a food as if it were harmful. Reactions can be mild or, sometimes, severe and life-threatening (anaphylaxis). Common triggers include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, wheat and sesame.
symptoms: Itching or tingling in the mouth
Swelling of the lips, face, tongue or throat
Sneezing, runny nose or itchy eyes
Tummy pain, feeling sick, vomiting or diarrhoea
Severe reactions: difficulty breathing, wheezing, dizziness or collapse
causes: The immune system wrongly reacting to proteins in certain foods
Common triggers include milk, eggs, peanuts, tree nuts, fish, shellfish, wheat, soya and sesame
diagnosis: A doctor or allergy specialist uses your history of reactions, skin prick tests, blood tests and sometimes supervised food challenges.
treatment: Avoiding the food
Antihistamines for mild reactions
Adrenaline auto-injectors for people at risk of anaphylaxis
Specialist allergy care, sometimes including desensitisation treatment
selfCare: Read food labels carefully
Tell restaurants and schools about the allergy
Carry prescribed adrenaline auto-injectors at all times if you have them
Have an allergy action plan
prevention: For babies, follow current advice on introducing allergenic foods; ask a health professional if your baby has eczema or a known allergy
whenToSeeDoctor: You or your child react after eating a food
Mild reactions that keep happening
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing or wheezing
Swelling of the throat or tongue, or difficulty swallowing
Feeling faint, dizzy or collapsing
Signs of anaphylaxis: use an adrenaline auto-injector if available and call emergency services

name: Food poisoning
overview: Food poisoning is illness caused by eating food contaminated with germs such as bacteria or viruses. It is rarely serious and usually gets better within a week. Keeping hydrated is the most important thing.
symptoms: Feeling generally unwell, with aches or chills
causes: Bacteria such as Campylobacter, Salmonella, E. coli or Listeria
Viruses such as norovirus
Food that is undercooked, poorly stored or handled with unwashed hands
riskFactors: Age over 65 or very young children
Eating raw or undercooked meat, eggs or shellfish
diagnosis: Food poisoning is usually diagnosed from the symptoms; a stool sample may be tested if symptoms are severe or prolonged.
treatment: Rest and plenty of fluids
Oral rehydration solutions if at risk of dehydration
Antibiotics are only needed for some specific bacterial infections
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids, little and often
Eat when you feel able, starting with small, plain meals
Stay off work or school until 2 days after symptoms stop
prevention: Cook food thoroughly, especially meat and poultry
Keep raw and ready-to-eat foods apart
Refrigerate food promptly and respect use-by dates
whenToSeeDoctor: You are pregnant
You are worried about a baby or young child
Signs of dehydration
Vomiting for more than 2 days or diarrhoea for more than 7 days
You have a long-term condition or weakened immune system
emergencySigns: Vomiting blood or bloody diarrhoea
Severe stomach pain
Unable to keep any fluids down and not passing urine
Confusion or a stiff neck

name: Fungal nail infection
overview: Fungal nail infections are common, especially in toenails. They are not usually serious but can take a long time to treat.
symptoms: Discoloured nail, often white, black, yellow or green
Nail lifting from the nail bed
Pain or discomfort in some cases
causes: Fungal infection, often spreading from athlete's foot
Fungi that thrive in warm, moist places
diagnosis: A doctor may diagnose it by looking at the nail and sending a nail clipping for testing.
treatment: Antifungal nail paint from a pharmacy for mild infections
Antifungal tablets prescribed by a doctor
Laser treatment or nail removal in some cases
selfCare: Keep nails short and feet clean and dry
Wear clean socks every day
Treat athlete's foot promptly
prevention: Do not share nail clippers or towels
whenToSeeDoctor: Treatment from a pharmacy has not worked
The infection is spreading or painful
You have diabetes or a weakened immune system

name: Gallstones
overview: Gallstones are small stones that form in the gallbladder. They often cause no symptoms, but if one blocks a duct it can cause sudden, intense tummy pain. Surgery to remove the gallbladder may be recommended if they cause problems.
symptoms: Sudden intense pain in the upper right or centre of the tummy that can last minutes to hours
Pain spreading to the right shoulder or back
High temperature, yellowing skin or eyes, or dark urine if complications develop
causes: An imbalance in the substances that make up bile, such as too much cholesterol
The gallbladder not emptying properly
diagnosis: Gallstones are usually diagnosed with an ultrasound scan, alongside blood tests.
treatment: No treatment if there are no symptoms
Painkillers for attacks
Keyhole surgery to remove the gallbladder
Procedures to remove stones from the bile duct
selfCare: Eat a healthy, balanced diet
Lose weight gradually rather than quickly
prevention: Avoid crash diets and rapid weight loss
whenToSeeDoctor: Tummy pain that comes and goes, especially after eating
Repeated attacks of upper tummy pain
emergencySigns: Tummy pain lasting longer than 8 hours
High temperature with shivering
Yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes
Pain so intense you cannot find a comfortable position

name: Gastroenteritis (stomach bug)
overview: Gastroenteritis is an infection of the gut that causes diarrhoea and vomiting. It is very common and usually gets better within a few days without treatment. The main risk is dehydration, especially in babies and older people.
causes: Viruses such as norovirus or rotavirus
Bacteria or parasites, often from contaminated food or water
Spread by close contact, unwashed hands and contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Living or working in close communities such as care homes, schools or cruise ships
Travel to areas with unsafe drinking water
diagnosis: It is usually diagnosed from symptoms; a stool sample may be tested if symptoms are severe, long-lasting or after travel.
treatment: Fluids to prevent dehydration, including oral rehydration solutions
Rest at home
Paracetamol for pain or fever
Hospital treatment for severe dehydration
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids, little and often
Keep breastfeeding or bottle feeding babies
Eat when you feel able
Stay off school or work until 2 days after symptoms stop
prevention: Wash hands with soap and water (alcohol gel does not kill norovirus)
Clean surfaces with a bleach-based cleaner
Wash contaminated clothing and bedding on a hot wash
whenToSeeDoctor: Signs of dehydration such as passing little urine
Vomiting for more than 2 days or diarrhoea for more than 7 days
Blood in diarrhoea or bleeding from the bottom
You are worried about a baby under 12 months
You have a weakened immune system
emergencySigns: Vomiting blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Green or yellow-green vomit
A stiff neck and pain when looking at bright lights
Sudden severe headache or stomach pain
Very drowsy, confused or not passing urine all day

name: Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD)
overview: Generalised anxiety disorder is a long-term condition where you feel anxious about many different things, most days, and find it hard to control the worry. It is common and treatable with talking therapies, medicines and self-help.
symptoms: Persistent worry that is hard to control
Physical symptoms such as a fast heartbeat, muscle tension, sweating or dizziness
causes: A mix of genetic, biological and life experience factors
Stressful or traumatic experiences
Long-term health conditions or alcohol and drug use
riskFactors: Heavy alcohol, caffeine or drug use
Other mental health conditions such as depression
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses GAD by asking about symptoms, how long they have lasted and how they affect daily life.
treatment: Talking therapies such as CBT
Guided self-help programmes
Medicines such as certain antidepressants, prescribed by a doctor
selfCare: Regular exercise
Breathing and relaxation exercises
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Talk to someone you trust
Keep a regular sleep routine
prevention: Healthy routines for sleep and exercise
whenToSeeDoctor: Anxiety is affecting daily life
Worry has lasted for several weeks or months
Self-help has not worked
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Chest pain or breathlessness that could be a heart problem (do not assume it is anxiety)

name: Genital herpes
overview: Genital herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the herpes simplex virus. The virus stays in the body and can cause outbreaks of sores from time to time. There is no cure, but treatment can ease outbreaks and reduce how often they happen.
symptoms: Small blisters that burst to leave red, open sores around the genitals, bottom or thighs
Tingling, burning or itching around the genitals
Flu-like symptoms during the first outbreak
causes: Herpes simplex virus passed on through skin-to-skin contact during vaginal, anal or oral sex
Oral sex with someone who has a cold sore
diagnosis: A doctor or nurse at a sexual health clinic may diagnose herpes by looking at the sores and taking a swab.
treatment: Antiviral medicine to shorten outbreaks
Longer-term antiviral treatment for frequent outbreaks
Painkillers and soothing creams as advised
selfCare: Keep the area clean and dry
Apply ice wrapped in a cloth or petroleum jelly to sores
Pee in a bath or with water poured over the area to reduce pain
Avoid sex from first tingling until sores have fully healed
prevention: Avoid oral sex when you or a partner has a cold sore
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have genital herpes
You are pregnant and have symptoms
Outbreaks are frequent or severe
emergencySigns: Unable to pee
Severe headache with a stiff neck or confusion

name: Glaucoma
overview: Glaucoma is a group of eye conditions where the optic nerve is damaged, usually by fluid building up in the eye. It often develops slowly without symptoms, so regular eye tests are important. Early treatment can prevent sight loss.
symptoms: In acute glaucoma: sudden intense eye pain, red eye and headache
causes: Build-up of fluid in the eye that increases pressure and damages the optic nerve
Sometimes damage occurs with normal eye pressure
riskFactors: Being of African, Caribbean or Asian descent
diagnosis: Glaucoma is detected during eye tests by measuring eye pressure, examining the optic nerve, and testing the field of vision.
treatment: Eye drops to lower eye pressure
Laser treatment
Surgery to improve fluid drainage
selfCare: Use eye drops exactly as prescribed
Attend all follow-up appointments
Tell the driving authority if required in your country
prevention: Regular eye tests, especially if over 40 or with a family history
whenToSeeDoctor: You have a family history of glaucoma and have not had an eye test recently
Gradual changes in vision
emergencySigns: Sudden intense eye pain with a red eye
Sudden blurred vision or seeing halos around lights with headache, nausea or vomiting

name: Glue ear
overview: Glue ear is when the middle part of the ear fills with sticky fluid, which can affect hearing. It is common in young children and usually clears up on its own within 3 months.
symptoms: Hearing loss: turning up the TV, mishearing or not responding
Ringing or buzzing in the ears
causes: Fluid build-up in the middle ear, often after a cold or ear infection
The tube linking the ear and throat not draining properly
diagnosis: A GP looks in the ear and may refer for hearing tests.
treatment: Watchful waiting, as it often clears within 3 months
Grommets (small tubes) inserted in the eardrum if it persists
Hearing aids in some cases
Antibiotics are not usually helpful
selfCare: Speak clearly and face your child when talking
Reduce background noise
Tell the school or nursery
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has hearing problems
Speech or behaviour concerns
Ear pain or discharge
emergencySigns: Swelling or redness behind the ear with fever
Severe headache, stiff neck or drowsiness

name: Gonorrhoea
overview: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria. Many people have no symptoms. It is treated with antibiotics, but resistance to some antibiotics is a growing concern, so follow-up testing may be advised.
symptoms: Often no symptoms, especially in women
Thick green or yellow discharge from the vagina or penis
Pain or discomfort in the bottom
causes: Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria passed on through unprotected vaginal, oral or anal sex
Sharing sex toys
From mother to baby during birth
diagnosis: Gonorrhoea is diagnosed with a swab or urine test at a sexual health clinic or GP.
treatment: Antibiotics, usually given by injection, at a sexual health clinic
A follow-up test may be advised to confirm the infection has gone
Partners should be tested and treated
selfCare: Avoid sex until treatment is complete and you have been told the infection has cleared
Tell recent sexual partners
whenToSeeDoctor: You have symptoms of an STI
A partner has gonorrhoea
You have had unprotected sex with a new partner
emergencySigns: Severe tummy pain with fever
Hot, swollen, painful joints with fever and skin spots

name: Gout
overview: Gout is a type of arthritis where crystals form inside joints, causing sudden attacks of severe pain and swelling. It often affects the big toe. Attacks can be treated, and long-term medicines and lifestyle changes help prevent them.
symptoms: Sudden severe pain in a joint, often the big toe
Hot, swollen, red skin over the joint (may be less visible on darker skin)
Extreme tenderness, even to light touch
causes: Too much uric acid in the blood, which forms crystals in the joints
Triggers include alcohol, sugary drinks, some foods such as red meat and seafood, and some medicines
riskFactors: High blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease
Drinking alcohol, especially beer and spirits
diagnosis: Gout is diagnosed from symptoms and a blood test for uric acid; sometimes fluid is taken from the joint to look for crystals.
treatment: Anti-inflammatory medicines or steroids to treat attacks
Long-term medicines to lower uric acid, prescribed by a doctor
Lifestyle changes
selfCare: Rest and raise the joint during an attack
Use an ice pack wrapped in a towel
Drink plenty of water
Cut down on alcohol and sugary drinks
prevention: Take uric acid-lowering medicine as prescribed
whenToSeeDoctor: Sudden severe joint pain
Repeated attacks
Attacks not improving with treatment
emergencySigns: A hot, painful joint with high temperature and feeling unwell (possible joint infection)

name: Haemorrhoids (piles)
overview: Haemorrhoids are lumps inside and around the bottom (anus) made of swollen blood vessels. They are very common and often get better by themselves after a few days. Simple self-care and pharmacy treatments usually help.
symptoms: Feeling like you still need to poo after going
Slimy mucus in underwear or on toilet paper
causes: Straining on the toilet, often due to constipation
Pressure on the veins in the bottom
diagnosis: A GP may examine the bottom, sometimes with a gloved finger, to check for piles and rule out other causes of bleeding.
treatment: Creams, ointments or suppositories from a pharmacy
Laxatives for constipation
Hospital procedures such as banding for persistent piles
Surgery in some cases
selfCare: Drink lots of fluids and eat high-fibre foods to keep poo soft
Wipe gently with damp toilet paper
Take a warm bath to ease itching and pain
Do not strain or delay going to the toilet
prevention: High-fibre diet and plenty of fluids
whenToSeeDoctor: No improvement after 7 days of treatment
Piles keep coming back
Blood in your poo, or poo that is dark or black, to rule out other causes
A change in bowel habits
emergencySigns: Bleeding that will not stop
Lots of blood, such as the toilet water turning red or large clots
Severe pain with high temperature

name: Hand, foot and mouth disease
overview: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a common infection in young children that causes mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet. It usually gets better on its own within 7 to 10 days. It is not related to foot and mouth disease in animals.
symptoms: A rash of spots or blisters on the hands, feet and sometimes the bottom or legs
Spots may be red, or darker or grey on darker skin
causes: Infection with enteroviruses such as coxsackievirus
Spread through coughs, sneezes, poo and fluid from blisters
diagnosis: It is diagnosed from the typical spots and mouth ulcers.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever
Mouth gels or sprays for ulcers, as advised by a pharmacist
selfCare: Drink fluids, such as water or milk, to avoid dehydration
Eat soft foods and avoid hot, spicy or acidic food
Wash hands often
prevention: Wash hands with soap and water, especially after nappy changes and the toilet
Do not share towels or utensils
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms not improving after 10 days
Your child is not drinking or has fewer wet nappies
Your child has a weakened immune system
You are pregnant and have been in contact with it
emergencySigns: Your child is floppy, very drowsy or unresponsive
A stiff neck or seizures
Difficulty breathing

sources.label: NHS: Hand, foot and mouth disease

name: Hay fever
overview: Hay fever is an allergic reaction to pollen, usually worse between late March and September in temperate climates. It causes sneezing, a runny nose and itchy eyes. It cannot be cured, but symptoms can be eased with pharmacy treatments.
symptoms: Itchy throat, mouth, nose and ears
causes: An allergic reaction to pollen from trees, grass or weeds
The immune system overreacting to a harmless substance
riskFactors: Living in areas with high pollen
diagnosis: Hay fever is usually diagnosed from symptoms and when they happen; allergy testing is rarely needed.
treatment: Antihistamine tablets, drops or nasal sprays
Steroid nasal sprays
Immunotherapy for severe cases, under a specialist
selfCare: Check pollen forecasts
Put petroleum jelly around nostrils to trap pollen
Wear wraparound sunglasses
Shower and change clothes after being outside
Keep windows and doors shut on high pollen days
prevention: Start treatment before the pollen season if advised
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms not improving with pharmacy medicines
Breathing problems such as wheezing or a tight chest
emergencySigns: Severe difficulty breathing or wheezing
Swelling of the lips, tongue or throat

name: Head lice and nits
