overview: Head lice are tiny insects that live in hair, and nits are their empty egg cases. They are very common in children and are not a sign of poor hygiene. They can be treated at home with wet combing or pharmacy treatments.
symptoms: Feeling like something is moving in the hair
Live lice in the hair, found by combing
Nits (empty egg cases) attached to hair close to the scalp
causes: Lice spreading by direct head-to-head contact
They cannot jump, fly or swim
diagnosis: Head lice are confirmed by finding live lice using a detection comb on wet or dry hair.
treatment: Wet combing with a special detection comb, repeated over 2 weeks
Lotions or sprays from a pharmacy
Treating everyone in the household found to have live lice on the same day
selfCare: Use conditioner and a fine-toothed comb to wet comb
Check the whole family
Repeat combing as instructed
prevention: There is no need to keep children off school
whenToSeeDoctor: Treatment has not worked after several attempts
The scalp is very sore or looks infected

name: Hearing loss
overview: Hearing loss is very common, especially as people get older. It can happen gradually or suddenly. Sometimes it is temporary and treatable, such as from earwax, and hearing aids help many people with long-term hearing loss.
symptoms: Difficulty hearing other people clearly or misunderstanding them
Turning the TV up louder than others want
Difficulty hearing on the phone or in noisy places
causes: Ageing
Exposure to loud noise
Earwax build-up
Ear infections or glue ear
Some medicines or conditions such as Ménière's disease
riskFactors: Loud noise exposure at work or leisure
diagnosis: A GP looks in the ears and refers for hearing tests by an audiologist if needed.
treatment: Removing earwax
Treating infections
Hearing aids
Cochlear implants for severe hearing loss
selfCare: Protect ears from loud noise
Do not use cotton buds in the ears
Ask people to face you when speaking
prevention: Have hearing checked if you notice changes
whenToSeeDoctor: Hearing is gradually getting worse
Hearing loss in one ear
Hearing loss with ear pain or discharge
emergencySigns: Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears (seek urgent help the same day)
Hearing loss after a head injury
Hearing loss with sudden dizziness, weakness or facial drooping

name: Heart attack
overview: A heart attack is a medical emergency where the blood supply to part of the heart is suddenly blocked, usually by a blood clot. Calling emergency services immediately saves lives and heart muscle. Treatment and rehabilitation help people recover and prevent another attack.
symptoms: Chest pain: pressure, tightness or squeezing in the centre of the chest
Pain spreading to the arms, neck, jaw, back or tummy
causes: Usually coronary heart disease, where a fatty plaque in an artery bursts and a clot forms
Less commonly, a spasm or tear in a coronary artery
riskFactors: High blood pressure, high cholesterol and diabetes
diagnosis: A heart attack is diagnosed in hospital with an ECG and blood tests that measure heart muscle damage.
treatment: Emergency treatment to restore blood flow, such as a stent procedure or clot-dissolving medicine
Medicines to protect the heart and prevent another heart attack
Cardiac rehabilitation programme
selfCare: Call emergency services straight away if you suspect a heart attack
While waiting, sit down and rest; chew aspirin only if advised by the call handler and not allergic
Take part in cardiac rehabilitation after a heart attack
prevention: Healthy diet, weight and regular activity
Control blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Chest discomfort that comes and goes with activity (possible angina)
After a heart attack, any new or worsening symptoms
emergencySigns: Chest pain or pressure that does not go away
Chest pain with breathlessness, sweating or feeling sick
Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back
Collapse or unconsciousness

name: Heart failure
overview: Heart failure means the heart is not pumping blood around the body as well as it should. It is a long-term condition that usually gets worse over time, but treatment can control symptoms for many years and help people live well.
symptoms: Breathlessness after activity or at rest
Feeling tired most of the time
Breathlessness when lying down or waking at night breathless
causes: Coronary heart disease and previous heart attacks
High blood pressure
Problems with heart muscle (cardiomyopathy) or heart valves
Irregular heart rhythms such as atrial fibrillation
riskFactors: Coronary heart disease or past heart attack
diagnosis: Heart failure is diagnosed with blood tests, an ECG and an echocardiogram (heart ultrasound).
treatment: Medicines to help the heart work better and reduce fluid build-up
Devices such as pacemakers or implantable defibrillators in some people
Surgery or procedures for valve or artery problems
Heart failure rehabilitation
selfCare: Weigh yourself daily if advised, as sudden gain can mean fluid build-up
Take medicines as prescribed
Stay active within your limits
Limit salt and alcohol and stop smoking
prevention: Treat coronary heart disease risk factors
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent breathlessness or tiredness
Swollen ankles or legs
Symptoms getting worse if you already have heart failure
Rapid weight gain over a few days
emergencySigns: Severe breathlessness or struggling to breathe
Chest pain
Coughing up frothy pink mucus
Fainting or collapse

name: Hepatitis A
overview: Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by a virus spread through contaminated food, water or close contact. It usually clears up on its own within a few months and does not cause long-term liver disease. A vaccine is available.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as tiredness, fever and aches
Loss of appetite and feeling sick
Pain in the upper right tummy
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
causes: Hepatitis A virus spread when tiny amounts of infected stool get into the mouth
Contaminated food or water, especially in areas with poor sanitation
Close contact with an infected person
riskFactors: Travel to areas where hepatitis A is common
Close contact with someone who has it
Men who have sex with men
diagnosis: Hepatitis A is diagnosed with a blood test.
treatment: No specific treatment; the infection usually clears on its own
Rest, fluids and relief of symptoms
Avoid alcohol and check with a doctor before taking medicines
selfCare: Rest and eat small, light meals
Avoid alcohol
Wash hands thoroughly and do not prepare food for others while infectious
prevention: Hepatitis A vaccine for travellers and people at higher risk
Wash hands after the toilet and before preparing food
whenToSeeDoctor: Yellowing of the skin or eyes
Symptoms of hepatitis after travel or contact with an infected person
emergencySigns: Confusion or extreme drowsiness
Vomiting blood or black stools
Severe tummy pain

name: Hepatitis B
overview: Hepatitis B is a liver infection caused by a virus spread through blood and body fluids. Adults usually clear it within a few months, but it can become a long-term (chronic) infection, especially when caught in infancy. A safe and effective vaccine is available.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as tiredness and fever
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
causes: Hepatitis B virus passed on through blood, semen and vaginal fluids
From mother to baby around birth
Unprotected sex or sharing needles
riskFactors: Being born to a mother with hepatitis B
Unprotected sex with an infected partner
Living in or coming from an area where hepatitis B is common
Unsterile tattooing, piercing or medical equipment
diagnosis: Hepatitis B is diagnosed with blood tests, which also show whether the infection is recent or chronic.
treatment: Short-term infections often need only symptom relief
Antiviral medicines for chronic hepatitis B to control the virus and protect the liver
Regular monitoring of liver health
selfCare: Avoid alcohol
Use condoms and do not share razors or toothbrushes
Attend regular check-ups
prevention: Hepatitis B vaccine, including for babies
Vaccination and treatment of babies born to mothers with hepatitis B
Use condoms and never share needles
whenToSeeDoctor: You may have been exposed (urgent vaccination can help prevent infection)
Symptoms of hepatitis such as jaundice
You are pregnant and have not been tested
emergencySigns: Confusion or extreme drowsiness
Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools
Severe tummy swelling or pain

name: Hepatitis C
overview: Hepatitis C is a virus spread mainly through blood that can infect and damage the liver. It often causes no symptoms for many years. Modern antiviral tablets can cure most people.
symptoms: Yellowing of the skin or eyes in later stages
causes: Hepatitis C virus spread through blood-to-blood contact
Sharing needles or drug equipment
Unsterile tattooing, piercing or medical procedures
riskFactors: Injecting drugs, now or in the past
Blood transfusions or medical treatment in countries where screening is limited
Sharing razors or toothbrushes with an infected person
diagnosis: Hepatitis C is diagnosed with blood tests: an antibody test, then a test for the virus itself.
treatment: Antiviral tablets taken for several weeks, which cure most people
Monitoring and care for any liver damage
selfCare: Avoid alcohol
Do not share razors, toothbrushes or needles
Keep a healthy weight
prevention: Never share needles or drug equipment
Use licensed tattoo and piercing studios
Testing for people at higher risk
whenToSeeDoctor: You have ever been at risk of infection and have not been tested
Persistent tiredness or symptoms of liver problems
emergencySigns: Vomiting blood or black stools
Confusion or extreme drowsiness
Rapidly swelling tummy

name: High blood pressure (hypertension)
overview: High blood pressure means the force of blood against the artery walls is consistently too high. It rarely causes symptoms, so the only way to know is to have it measured. Left untreated it raises the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney disease, but lifestyle changes and medicines can control it.
symptoms: Very high blood pressure can occasionally cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain
causes: Often no single cause, but linked to lifestyle and genes
Being overweight, eating too much salt and not exercising enough
Drinking too much alcohol and smoking
Some conditions such as kidney disease, or certain medicines
riskFactors: Family history of high blood pressure
Being of Black African or Black Caribbean descent
High-salt diet, low physical activity, alcohol and smoking
diagnosis: Blood pressure is measured with a cuff on several occasions; home or 24-hour ambulatory monitoring is often used to confirm the diagnosis.
treatment: Lifestyle changes: less salt, healthy diet, more activity, less alcohol, stopping smoking
Blood pressure-lowering medicines prescribed by a doctor
Regular blood pressure checks
selfCare: Cut down on salt
Be active most days
Keep to a healthy weight
Limit alcohol and stop smoking
Check blood pressure at home if advised
prevention: Healthy, balanced diet with plenty of fruit and vegetables
Regular blood pressure checks, especially over 40
whenToSeeDoctor: You are over 40 and have not had your blood pressure checked recently
Home readings are consistently high
Side effects from blood pressure medicines
emergencySigns: Very high reading with chest pain, shortness of breath or severe headache
Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness or speech problems
Sudden changes in vision or confusion

name: High cholesterol
overview: Cholesterol is a fatty substance in the blood. Too much of it can build up in the arteries and raise the risk of heart attack and stroke. It does not usually cause symptoms and is found with a blood test.
symptoms: It is often found only through a blood test or after a heart attack or stroke
Very high inherited cholesterol can occasionally cause fatty lumps on tendons or yellowish patches around the eyes
causes: Eating a lot of saturated fat
Not exercising enough, being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol
Inherited conditions such as familial hypercholesterolaemia
Other conditions such as diabetes, kidney disease or an underactive thyroid
riskFactors: Family history of high cholesterol or early heart disease
diagnosis: High cholesterol is diagnosed with a blood test, often as part of a routine health check alongside an assessment of overall heart risk.
treatment: Diet and lifestyle changes
Cholesterol-lowering medicines such as statins, prescribed by a doctor
Treating linked conditions such as diabetes
selfCare: Eat less saturated fat and more fibre, fruit, vegetables and oily fish
Exercise regularly
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
prevention: Regular checks if you are at higher risk
whenToSeeDoctor: You are over 40 and have not had a cholesterol test
A family history of high cholesterol or early heart disease
You are overweight or have diabetes or high blood pressure
emergencySigns: Chest pain or pressure, which could be a heart attack
Sudden face drooping, arm weakness or speech problems (possible stroke)

name: HIV
overview: HIV is a virus that damages the immune system. There is no cure, but effective treatment keeps the virus under control so people can live long, healthy lives. People on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on through sex.
symptoms: Many people have no symptoms for years
A short flu-like illness a few weeks after infection: fever, sore throat and rash
Without treatment, later: weight loss, recurring infections, night sweats and swollen glands
causes: HIV passed on through blood, semen, vaginal and anal fluids, and breast milk
Most commonly through sex without a condom
Sharing needles
From mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding if untreated
riskFactors: Sex without a condom with a partner of unknown or detectable HIV status
diagnosis: HIV is diagnosed with a blood test or a finger-prick or saliva test; testing is free and confidential at sexual health clinics.
treatment: Antiretroviral medicines taken every day for life
Regular check-ups to monitor the immune system and viral load
selfCare: Take treatment every day as prescribed
Stay up to date with recommended vaccines
Keep a healthy lifestyle and attend check-ups
prevention: Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for people at higher risk
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours of possible exposure
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have been exposed to HIV (go within 72 hours for PEP)
You have had unprotected sex or shared needles and have not been tested
Flu-like illness after a possible exposure
emergencySigns: Severe difficulty breathing
Seizures, confusion or severe headache
Very high fever with feeling extremely unwell

name: HPV and genital warts
overview: HPV is a very common group of viruses spread through skin-to-skin contact, including during sex. Most infections cause no symptoms and clear on their own, but some types cause genital warts and others can lead to cancers such as cervical cancer. The HPV vaccine protects against the most harmful types.
symptoms: Genital warts: small, painless growths or lumps around the genitals or anus
causes: Human papillomavirus spread through skin-to-skin contact of the genital area
Vaginal, anal or oral sex and sharing sex toys
riskFactors: Smoking or a weakened immune system (harder to clear the virus)
diagnosis: Genital warts are diagnosed by examination at a sexual health clinic; high-risk HPV is checked through cervical screening.
treatment: Creams or liquids applied to warts, prescribed by a clinician
Freezing, heating or removing warts at a clinic
Follow-up of abnormal cervical screening results
selfCare: Do not use over-the-counter wart treatments meant for hands or feet on genital warts
Use condoms during treatment
prevention: Use condoms (reduces but does not fully remove risk)
whenToSeeDoctor: You notice lumps or growths around the genitals or anus
You are invited for cervical screening
Unusual bleeding, such as after sex or between periods

name: Impetigo
overview: Impetigo is a common and contagious skin infection that causes sores and blisters. It is most common in young children. It is not usually serious and often improves within a week of treatment.
symptoms: Red sores or blisters that burst and leave crusty, golden-brown patches
Often around the nose and mouth, but can be anywhere
causes: Bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus infecting the skin
Often through broken skin from cuts, insect bites or eczema
riskFactors: Close contact settings such as nurseries and schools
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses impetigo by looking at the sores; a swab may be taken if it keeps coming back.
treatment: Antiseptic or antibiotic cream prescribed by a doctor or recommended by a pharmacist
Antibiotic tablets if widespread or severe
selfCare: Wash sores gently with warm soapy water
Avoid touching or scratching sores
Do not share towels or flannels
Stay off school or work until sores have crusted and healed, or 48 hours after starting antibiotics
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you or your child has impetigo
Symptoms do not improve within 7 days of treatment
Impetigo keeps coming back
emergencySigns: Sores spreading rapidly with high temperature and feeling very unwell

name: Insomnia
overview: Insomnia means regularly having problems getting to sleep or staying asleep, and feeling tired during the day. It is common and often improves with changes to sleep habits. Talking therapy for insomnia is the main long-term treatment.
symptoms: Waking several times in the night or too early
Feeling tired and irritable during the day
causes: Stress, anxiety or depression
Noise, light or an uncomfortable bedroom
Alcohol, caffeine or nicotine
Shift work or jet lag
Physical health problems or some medicines
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses insomnia by asking about sleep habits and daily routine, sometimes using a sleep diary.
treatment: Improving sleep habits
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)
Treating any underlying cause
Sleeping tablets only rarely and for a short time
selfCare: Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day
Relax before bed and avoid screens
Keep the bedroom dark, quiet and cool
Avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals late in the evening
Exercise regularly, but not just before bed
whenToSeeDoctor: Sleep problems lasting more than a few weeks despite changes
Insomnia affecting daily life
Loud snoring or gasping during sleep
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm

name: Iron deficiency anaemia
overview: Iron deficiency anaemia is when a lack of iron means the body cannot make enough healthy red blood cells. It is common and can make you feel tired and short of breath. It is usually easy to treat, but the cause should be found.
symptoms: Craving non-food items such as ice (pica)
causes: Heavy periods
Pregnancy
Bleeding in the gut, for example from ulcers or bowel cancer
Not enough iron in the diet
Conditions that stop the body absorbing iron, such as coeliac disease
riskFactors: Vegetarian or vegan diet without enough iron-rich foods
diagnosis: Anaemia is diagnosed with a blood test; further tests may be needed to find the cause of the iron deficiency.
treatment: Iron tablets or liquid prescribed by a doctor
Iron given into a vein in some cases
Treating the underlying cause, such as heavy periods or bleeding
selfCare: Eat iron-rich foods such as dark green leafy vegetables, beans, fortified cereals, meat and dried fruit
Take iron supplements as directed
Avoid tea or coffee with meals, which can reduce iron absorption
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms of anaemia such as tiredness and breathlessness
Heavy periods
Symptoms not improving after treatment
emergencySigns: Chest pain or severe breathlessness
Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools
Fainting

name: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
overview: IBS is a common, long-term condition of the digestive system that causes tummy pain, bloating and changes in bowel habit. It does not damage the gut, and symptoms often come and go. Diet and lifestyle changes help many people.
symptoms: Tummy pain or cramps, often eased by pooing
Diarrhoea, constipation, or both at different times
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Linked to how the gut and brain communicate, gut sensitivity and how quickly food moves through the gut
Can start after a gut infection
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses IBS from symptoms and may do blood and stool tests to rule out other conditions such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease.
treatment: Diet changes, sometimes with help from a dietitian (for example a low FODMAP diet)
Medicines for diarrhoea, constipation or cramps
Talking therapies such as CBT or gut-directed hypnotherapy
selfCare: Keep a food and symptom diary
Eat regular meals and do not skip them
Adjust fibre intake depending on symptoms
Exercise and find ways to manage stress
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have IBS
Symptoms change or get worse
Pharmacy remedies are not helping
emergencySigns: Bleeding from the bottom or bloody diarrhoea
Severe tummy pain that does not go away
Unexplained weight loss with feeling very unwell

name: Kidney stones
overview: Kidney stones are hard deposits that form in the kidneys from waste products in the blood. Small stones often pass out in urine on their own, but larger ones can cause severe pain and may need treatment.
symptoms: Severe pain in the side of the tummy or back that may spread to the groin
Feeling restless and unable to get comfortable
Needing to pee more often or pain when peeing
causes: Waste chemicals such as calcium or uric acid building up and forming crystals
Not drinking enough fluids, making urine concentrated
riskFactors: A diet high in salt or animal protein
Family history or previous kidney stones
diagnosis: Kidney stones are diagnosed with urine and blood tests and a scan, usually a CT scan.
treatment: Painkillers and anti-sickness medicines
Medicines to help stones pass
Procedures to break up or remove larger stones, such as shockwave treatment or ureteroscopy
selfCare: Drink plenty of water throughout the day so urine is pale
Strain your urine if advised, to collect the stone for testing
prevention: Follow specific diet advice for your stone type
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain in the side or back that comes and goes
Blood in urine
Recurring urine infections
emergencySigns: Severe pain with high temperature and shivering
Pain so severe you cannot get comfortable or stop vomiting
Unable to pee

name: Lung cancer
overview: Lung cancer is one of the most common and serious cancers. Smoking is the main cause, but people who have never smoked can also get it. It often has no symptoms early on, so getting persistent symptoms checked is important.
symptoms: A cough that lasts more than 3 weeks or changes
Chest infections that keep coming back
causes: Smoking, the main cause
Exposure to second-hand smoke, radon gas, asbestos and air pollution
riskFactors: Smoking, now or in the past
Workplace exposure to asbestos and other chemicals
diagnosis: Lung cancer is diagnosed with a chest X-ray, CT scan and a biopsy; some countries offer lung screening for people at high risk.
treatment: Surgery
Radiotherapy
Chemotherapy
Targeted medicines and immunotherapy
selfCare: Stop smoking, at any stage
Stay active and eat well during treatment
prevention: Do not smoke and avoid second-hand smoke
Test your home for radon where advised
whenToSeeDoctor: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Coughing up blood
Unexplained breathlessness, weight loss or tiredness
emergencySigns: Coughing up a lot of blood
Severe difficulty breathing
Sudden swelling of the face and neck

name: Lupus (SLE)
overview: Lupus is a long-term condition where the immune system attacks healthy tissue, causing inflammation in the joints, skin and other organs. Symptoms often come and go in flares. Treatment can control symptoms and protect organs.
symptoms: Rashes, often across the cheeks and nose or on sun-exposed skin
causes: The immune system attacking the body's own tissues (an autoimmune condition)
A combination of genetic, hormonal and environmental factors such as sunlight or infections
riskFactors: Being of African, Caribbean, Asian or Hispanic descent
diagnosis: Lupus is diagnosed by a specialist using symptoms, examination and blood and urine tests, including antibody tests.
treatment: Antimalarial medicines used to treat lupus
Anti-inflammatory medicines and steroids
Immunosuppressants and biological medicines
Regular monitoring of kidneys and other organs
selfCare: Protect skin from the sun
Balance activity with rest
Stop smoking
Learn to spot signs of a flare
prevention: Sun protection and avoiding known triggers can reduce flares
whenToSeeDoctor: Ongoing joint pain, tiredness and rashes
Symptoms of a flare if you have lupus
Swelling of the legs or foamy urine
emergencySigns: Chest pain or severe breathlessness
Seizures or sudden confusion
Signs of stroke
High fever with feeling very unwell while on immune-suppressing medicines

name: Lyme disease
overview: Lyme disease is a bacterial infection spread to humans by infected ticks. It is easier to treat if diagnosed early. The classic first sign is a circular red rash around a tick bite.
symptoms: A circular or oval rash around a tick bite, which may look like a bull's-eye and spreads over days
Flu-like symptoms such as high temperature, headache and tiredness
Later, if untreated: facial weakness, nerve pain or joint swelling
causes: Borrelia bacteria passed on by the bite of an infected tick
Ticks are found in grassy and wooded areas and are more active in spring and summer
riskFactors: Spending time in woodland, heath or long grass where ticks live
Not checking for and removing ticks promptly
diagnosis: A doctor can diagnose Lyme disease from the typical rash; blood tests may be used if there is no rash.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor, usually for a few weeks
Longer or intravenous antibiotics for some later-stage symptoms, guided by a specialist
selfCare: Remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool, gripping close to the skin
Clean the bite area and watch for a rash over the following weeks
prevention: Cover skin and use insect repellent in tick areas
Check skin and clothing for ticks after being outdoors
whenToSeeDoctor: A rash appears after a tick bite
Flu-like symptoms after a tick bite or time in tick areas
emergencySigns: Chest pain, palpitations or fainting
Weakness of the face with severe headache or stiff neck

name: Malaria
overview: Malaria is a serious infection caused by parasites spread through the bites of infected mosquitoes. It is common in parts of Africa, Asia and South and Central America. It can be life-threatening but is preventable and curable if treated promptly.
symptoms: Symptoms can appear weeks or even months after travel
causes: Plasmodium parasites passed on by the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes
Rarely, through blood transfusion or from mother to baby during pregnancy
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to areas where malaria is common
Not taking antimalarial tablets when advised
diagnosis: Malaria is diagnosed with a blood test, either under a microscope or with a rapid diagnostic test; mention any recent travel.
treatment: Antimalarial medicines prescribed by a doctor, chosen by the type of parasite and where it was caught
Hospital treatment for severe malaria
selfCare: Seek medical help urgently if you develop a fever during or after travel to a malaria area
Finish all medicines as prescribed
prevention: Get travel health advice before travelling
Use insect repellent, cover up and sleep under a mosquito net
Malaria vaccines for children in some high-risk countries
whenToSeeDoctor: Fever or flu-like symptoms during or within a year of visiting a malaria area: get medical help the same day
You are planning travel to a malaria area (get advice on prevention before you go)
emergencySigns: Confusion, drowsiness or seizures
Difficulty breathing
Yellowing of the skin or eyes with feeling very unwell
Dark urine or passing little urine
Collapse

name: Measles
overview: Measles is a highly infectious viral illness that can be very unpleasant and sometimes lead to serious problems. It starts with cold-like symptoms followed by a rash. Two doses of the MMR vaccine give strong protection.
symptoms: Runny or blocked nose, sneezing and cough
Small white spots inside the cheeks
A blotchy rash starting on the face and behind the ears, then spreading
causes: Infection with the measles virus
Spread through the air from coughs and sneezes of an infected person
riskFactors: Babies too young for the vaccine
diagnosis: A doctor suspects measles from the symptoms and confirms it with a saliva, swab or blood test; call ahead before visiting so you can be kept apart from others.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral cure; care focuses on easing symptoms
Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen
Hospital treatment for complications
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Stay away from nursery, school or work for at least 4 days after the rash appears
Avoid contact with babies, pregnant people and people with weak immunity
prevention: Two doses of the MMR vaccine
whenToSeeDoctor: You or your child might have measles (phone first)
You have been in contact with someone with measles and are not fully vaccinated, are pregnant, or have weak immunity
A baby has been in contact with measles
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing
Chest pain
Seizures or confusion
Very drowsy or hard to wake
Coughing up blood

name: Melanoma skin cancer
overview: Melanoma is a type of skin cancer that can spread to other parts of the body. It often appears as a new mole or a change in an existing mole. The main cause is ultraviolet light from the sun or sunbeds, and it is very treatable when found early.
symptoms: A new mole or a change in an existing mole
A mole with an uneven shape or border
A mole that is getting bigger
A mole that is itchy, crusting or bleeding
Can appear anywhere, including under nails and on the soles of the feet
causes: Damage to skin cells from ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun or sunbeds
Genetic factors
riskFactors: Lots of moles or unusual moles
History of sunburn or sunbed use
diagnosis: A doctor examines the skin and refers to a skin specialist, who may remove the mole for testing (biopsy).
treatment: Surgery to remove the melanoma
Immunotherapy and targeted medicines for advanced melanoma
Radiotherapy in some cases
selfCare: Check your skin regularly for new or changing moles
Use sunscreen and protective clothing
prevention: Avoid sunburn: seek shade, cover up and use high-factor sunscreen
whenToSeeDoctor: A new mole or a change in an existing mole
A mole that is bleeding, itchy or crusting
A dark streak under a nail

sources.label: National Cancer Institute: Skin Cancer (Including Melanoma)

name: Meningitis
overview: Meningitis is an infection of the protective layers around the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and can be life-threatening, while viral meningitis is usually milder. Vaccines protect against several causes.
symptoms: A rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it (not always present)
Stiff neck and dislike of bright lights
causes: Bacteria such as meningococcus or pneumococcus
Viruses
Spread by coughs, sneezes, kissing or close contact
riskFactors: Living in crowded settings such as student halls
diagnosis: Meningitis is diagnosed in hospital with blood tests and a lumbar puncture, where fluid is taken from the spine.
treatment: Urgent antibiotics in hospital for bacterial meningitis
Fluids, oxygen and other support in hospital
Viral meningitis usually gets better on its own with rest
selfCare: Do not wait for a rash to appear before getting help
Trust your instincts if someone seems seriously ill
prevention: Routine vaccines including MenB, MenACWY, Hib and pneumococcal
Antibiotics may be offered to close contacts of someone with bacterial meningitis
whenToSeeDoctor: Any suspicion of meningitis: get medical help immediately rather than waiting for a routine appointment
You have been in close contact with someone with bacterial meningitis
Ongoing problems such as hearing loss or headaches after recovery
emergencySigns: Rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Stiff neck and severe headache
Drowsiness, confusion or being hard to wake
Seizures
In babies: a bulging soft spot, floppiness or a high-pitched cry

name: Menopause
overview: Menopause is when periods stop due to lower hormone levels, usually between ages 45 and 55. Perimenopause is the time before, when symptoms often start. Symptoms can be managed with lifestyle changes and treatments such as hormone replacement therapy.
symptoms: Changes to periods, becoming irregular before stopping
Low mood, anxiety or mood swings
Vaginal dryness and reduced sex drive
causes: Natural fall in oestrogen and other hormones with age
Surgery to remove the ovaries
Some cancer treatments
riskFactors: Early menopause can run in families
diagnosis: Menopause is usually diagnosed from symptoms in people over 45; blood tests may be used in younger people.
treatment: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)
Non-hormonal medicines for hot flushes
Vaginal oestrogen or lubricants for dryness
Talking therapies such as CBT for mood and sleep
selfCare: Regular exercise
Healthy diet with enough calcium and vitamin D
Wear light layers and keep the bedroom cool
Limit caffeine, alcohol and spicy food if they trigger flushes
prevention: Menopause is natural and cannot be prevented, but bone and heart health can be protected with exercise and a healthy diet
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms affecting your daily life
Symptoms of menopause before age 45
Bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months

name: Migraine
overview: A migraine is usually a moderate or severe headache felt as a throbbing pain on one side of the head, often with feeling sick and sensitivity to light or sound. It is a common condition. Treatments can ease attacks and reduce how often they happen.
symptoms: Throbbing headache, often on one side
Sensitivity to light, sound or smells
Visual disturbances (aura) such as flashing lights or zigzags before the headache
Numbness, tingling or difficulty speaking during an aura
Tiredness before or after an attack
causes: Not fully understood, thought to involve changes in brain activity, nerves and blood vessels
Triggers such as stress, poor sleep, hormonal changes, missed meals, dehydration and some foods or alcohol
diagnosis: Migraine is diagnosed from the pattern of symptoms and an examination; scans are usually only needed if there are unusual features.
treatment: Painkillers such as paracetamol, ibuprofen or aspirin taken early in an attack
Triptan medicines prescribed by a doctor
Anti-sickness medicines
Preventive medicines if attacks are frequent
selfCare: Rest in a quiet, dark room during an attack
Keep a migraine diary to identify triggers
Regular sleep, meals and fluids
Avoid taking painkillers on too many days, which can cause medication-overuse headaches
whenToSeeDoctor: Frequent or severe migraines
Painkillers are not helping
Symptoms on most days
Migraine pattern changes
emergencySigns: Sudden, extremely severe headache ('worst ever')
Headache with stiff neck, fever, confusion or rash
Weakness on one side, slurred speech or face drooping
Headache after a head injury
Loss of vision or seizures

name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
overview: Multiple sclerosis is a lifelong condition where the immune system damages the protective coating around nerves in the brain and spinal cord. It can cause a wide range of symptoms, which vary between people. Treatments can reduce relapses and help manage symptoms.
symptoms: Vision problems, such as blurred vision or pain moving the eye
Bladder problems and difficulty thinking or concentrating
causes: The immune system attacking the myelin coating of nerves (an autoimmune condition)
A mix of genetic and environmental factors, including low vitamin D, smoking and past Epstein-Barr virus infection
diagnosis: MS is diagnosed by a neurologist using a neurological examination, an MRI scan, and sometimes a lumbar puncture.
treatment: Disease-modifying medicines to reduce relapses
Steroids to speed recovery from relapses
Treatments for specific symptoms such as fatigue, spasms or bladder problems
Physiotherapy and rehabilitation
selfCare: Regular exercise
Balanced diet
Stop smoking
Plan rest to manage fatigue
prevention: There is no known way to prevent MS; not smoking may lower risk
whenToSeeDoctor: Vision problems, numbness, weakness or balance problems that last more than a day
New or worsening symptoms if you have MS
emergencySigns: Sudden weakness on one side, face drooping or slurred speech
Sudden severe loss of vision
Unable to pee

name: Nappy rash
overview: Nappy rash is very common in babies and young children. It causes red, sore patches on the skin in the nappy area. It can usually be treated at home with simple care and barrier creams.
symptoms: Red or darker patches on the bottom or genital area
causes: Skin in contact with wee or poo for a long time
Rubbing from the nappy
Soaps, bubble bath or wipes that irritate the skin
A fungal (thrush) infection in some cases
diagnosis: Nappy rash is recognised by looking at the skin; a GP or health visitor can check whether an infection is present.
treatment: Barrier cream applied at each nappy change
Antifungal cream if thrush is suspected, as advised by a pharmacist or GP
selfCare: Change nappies as soon as they are wet or dirty
Clean with water or fragrance-free wipes
Leave the nappy off for a while each day
Pat skin dry rather than rubbing
whenToSeeDoctor: The rash does not improve after a week of treatment
Your baby has a high temperature
The rash spreads or looks infected, with blisters or pus
emergencySigns: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Your baby is floppy, very drowsy or not feeding

name: Non-melanoma skin cancer
overview: Non-melanoma skin cancers, mainly basal cell and squamous cell carcinomas, are the most common types of skin cancer. They usually develop on skin often exposed to the sun and are very treatable, especially when found early.
symptoms: A lump or discoloured patch on the skin that does not heal after 4 weeks
A scab or sore that keeps coming back
A scaly, crusted patch that may bleed
Often on the face, ears, neck, lips, scalp or backs of the hands
causes: Long-term exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light from the sun or sunbeds, which damages skin cells
Less commonly, other factors such as previous radiotherapy or long-term immune suppression
riskFactors: Lots of sun exposure or sunbed use
A weakened immune system, for example after an organ transplant
diagnosis: A doctor examines the skin and may refer to a skin specialist for a biopsy.
treatment: Surgery to remove the cancer
Creams or freezing treatment for some early cancers
Radiotherapy or other treatments in some cases
selfCare: Check your skin regularly
Protect your skin from the sun
prevention: Seek shade, cover up and use high-factor sunscreen
whenToSeeDoctor: A skin lump, patch or sore that has not healed after 4 weeks
A sore that keeps coming back or bleeding

sources.label: National Cancer Institute: Skin Cancer (Including Melanoma)

name: Obesity
overview: Obesity means having a lot of body fat, enough to affect health. It raises the risk of conditions such as type 2 diabetes, heart disease, some cancers and joint problems. It is usually measured with body mass index (BMI) and waist size, and support is available to help.
symptoms: High BMI and large waist measurement
causes: Taking in more energy from food and drink than the body uses
Inactivity
Genes and some medical conditions or medicines
Environment and access to healthy food
riskFactors: Diet high in processed and sugary foods
Some medicines and conditions such as an underactive thyroid
diagnosis: A doctor measures height, weight and waist size to calculate BMI and assess health risks.
treatment: Healthy eating and increased physical activity
Weight management programmes and behavioural support
Weight-loss medicines prescribed by a doctor for some people
Weight-loss surgery in some cases
selfCare: Set realistic goals and aim for gradual weight loss
Eat more vegetables, fruit and wholegrains
Be active most days
Get support from local services or a GP
prevention: Limit sugary drinks and processed foods
whenToSeeDoctor: You are worried about your weight
You want support to lose weight
Symptoms such as breathlessness, joint pain or snoring

name: Obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD)
overview: OCD is a mental health condition where a person has unwanted, distressing thoughts (obsessions) and feels driven to carry out repetitive actions (compulsions) to relieve the anxiety. It can be very time-consuming, but treatment helps most people.
symptoms: Unwanted, intrusive thoughts, images or urges
Fear of contamination, harm or things not being right
Repetitive behaviours such as cleaning, checking or counting
Mental rituals such as repeating words
Spending a lot of time on rituals and feeling distressed
causes: Not fully understood
Genetics, brain differences and life experiences all play a part
riskFactors: Certain personality traits such as perfectionism
diagnosis: OCD is diagnosed by a GP or mental health professional through a conversation about thoughts, behaviours and their impact.
treatment: Talking therapy: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
Antidepressant medicines in some cases
Specialist services for severe OCD
selfCare: Learn about OCD
Practise resisting compulsions gradually with support
Join a support group
Look after sleep, activity and stress
prevention: Seeking help early can stop OCD getting worse
whenToSeeDoctor: Obsessions or compulsions are taking up a lot of time or causing distress
OCD is affecting work, school or relationships
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm

name: Obstructive sleep apnoea
overview: Obstructive sleep apnoea is when the throat walls relax and narrow during sleep, interrupting breathing. It causes loud snoring and daytime sleepiness. Treatment can improve sleep and lower risks such as high blood pressure and accidents.
symptoms: Breathing stopping and starting during sleep (often noticed by a partner)
Loud snoring, gasping or choking noises
Feeling very sleepy during the day
causes: The muscles and soft tissue in the throat relaxing and narrowing the airway during sleep
Extra tissue around the neck or a narrow airway, for example from overweight or large tonsils
riskFactors: Drinking alcohol or taking sedatives before bed
Enlarged tonsils or a small jaw
diagnosis: Sleep apnoea is diagnosed with a sleep study, often using a device worn at home overnight that measures breathing and oxygen levels.
treatment: Lifestyle changes such as weight loss and less alcohol
A CPAP machine that gently pumps air through a mask during sleep
A mouth device (mandibular advancement device) for some people
Surgery is rarely needed
selfCare: Lose weight if overweight
Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills before bed
Sleep on your side
Stop smoking
whenToSeeDoctor: Someone notices you stop breathing or gasp while asleep
You feel very tired during the day despite sleeping
You fall asleep at inappropriate times, such as while driving
emergencySigns: Chest pain or severe breathlessness
Being extremely drowsy and hard to wake

name: Osteoarthritis
overview: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis, causing joints to become painful and stiff. It most often affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. Exercise, weight management and pain relief help most people stay active.
symptoms: Joint pain and stiffness, often worse after rest or at the end of the day
A grating or crackling feeling in the joint
Weakness and loss of muscle around the joint
causes: Gradual damage to the cartilage lining the joint, with the body's repair process changing the joint
Previous joint injury or surgery
Other joint conditions such as gout or rheumatoid arthritis
riskFactors: Jobs involving repetitive stress on joints
diagnosis: A GP usually diagnoses osteoarthritis from symptoms and an examination; X-rays or blood tests are sometimes used to rule out other conditions.
treatment: Exercise and physiotherapy to strengthen muscles
Weight loss if overweight
Painkillers and anti-inflammatory creams or tablets
Steroid injections, or joint replacement surgery for severe cases
selfCare: Stay active with low-impact exercise such as walking, swimming or cycling
Keep to a healthy weight
Use supportive footwear
Use heat or cold packs for pain
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent joint pain or stiffness
Joint pain affecting daily activities
Pain not controlled by simple painkillers
emergencySigns: A hot, red, swollen joint with fever (possible joint infection)
Sudden inability to bear weight after a fall

name: Osteoporosis
overview: Osteoporosis is a condition that weakens bones, making them fragile and more likely to break. It develops slowly over years and is often only found after a fall or minor injury causes a fracture. Treatment and lifestyle changes help strengthen bones.
symptoms: Usually no symptoms until a bone breaks
Broken bones after a minor fall, often in the wrist, hip or spine
Loss of height or a stooped posture
Sudden back pain from a spinal fracture
causes: Natural bone loss with age
Hormonal changes, especially falling oestrogen after menopause
Some medicines such as long-term steroids
Medical conditions affecting hormones or nutrient absorption
riskFactors: Family history of osteoporosis or hip fracture
diagnosis: Osteoporosis is diagnosed with a bone density scan (DEXA), often alongside a fracture risk assessment.
treatment: Medicines to strengthen bones, prescribed by a doctor
Calcium and vitamin D supplements if needed
Hormone therapy for some people
Falls prevention
selfCare: Regular weight-bearing and muscle-strengthening exercise
Eat a diet rich in calcium
Get enough vitamin D
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Reduce fall risks at home
prevention: Calcium-rich diet and enough vitamin D
whenToSeeDoctor: You have risk factors and are worried
A bone breaks after a minor fall
Loss of height or curving of the spine
emergencySigns: Unable to stand or bear weight after a fall, or severe pain in the hip or back
A visibly deformed limb after a fall

name: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism)
overview: An overactive thyroid means the thyroid gland makes too much thyroid hormone. It can speed up many body functions. It is treatable with medicines, radioactive iodine or surgery.
symptoms: Swelling in the neck (goitre) or bulging eyes
causes: Graves' disease, where the immune system makes the thyroid overactive
Lumps (nodules) on the thyroid
Inflammation of the thyroid
Some medicines
diagnosis: An overactive thyroid is diagnosed with blood tests of thyroid hormone levels, sometimes with a scan.
treatment: Medicines that reduce thyroid hormone production
Medicines to control symptoms such as a fast heartbeat
Radioactive iodine treatment
Surgery to remove some or all of the thyroid
selfCare: Take medicines as prescribed
Attend regular blood tests
Stop smoking, especially if eyes are affected
prevention: There is no known way to prevent most causes
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms such as weight loss, a fast heartbeat or feeling anxious
Swelling in the neck
Eye problems such as bulging, sore or dry eyes
emergencySigns: Very fast heartbeat with high temperature, confusion or agitation (thyroid storm)
Chest pain or fainting
Sudden loss of vision or severe eye pain

name: Panic disorder
overview: Panic disorder is an anxiety condition where you have regular, sudden panic attacks, often for no obvious reason, and worry about having more. Panic attacks feel frightening but are not dangerous in themselves. Treatment is effective.
symptoms: Sudden intense fear or a sense of doom
Shortness of breath or feeling of choking
Chest pain, nausea or tingling fingers
causes: A mix of genetic and life experience factors
Stressful life events
Sensitivity to the body's stress responses
riskFactors: Heavy caffeine, alcohol or drug use
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses panic disorder from your description of attacks, and may do tests to rule out heart or thyroid problems.
treatment: Talking therapies such as CBT
Medicines such as certain antidepressants, prescribed by a doctor
Self-help programmes
selfCare: During an attack, stay where you are and breathe slowly and deeply
Remind yourself that the attack will pass
Regular exercise and relaxation
Limit caffeine and alcohol
whenToSeeDoctor: You have repeated panic attacks
Fear of attacks is stopping you doing things
You are avoiding places or situations
emergencySigns: Chest pain with sweating or pain spreading to the arm or jaw, especially if you have not had panic attacks before
Thoughts of suicide or self-harm

name: Parkinson's disease
overview: Parkinson's disease is a condition where parts of the brain become progressively damaged over many years, mainly affecting movement. There is no cure yet, but treatments help control symptoms and keep people active.
symptoms: Shaking (tremor), often starting in one hand
Loss of sense of smell, constipation, sleep problems and low mood
Memory or thinking problems later on
causes: Loss of nerve cells in the part of the brain that produces dopamine
Thought to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors
diagnosis: Parkinson's is diagnosed by a specialist from symptoms and an examination; there is no single test, and scans may be used to rule out other causes.
treatment: Medicines that replace or mimic dopamine
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy
Deep brain stimulation surgery for some people
selfCare: Stay as physically active as possible
Eat a balanced, high-fibre diet
Take medicines on time
Make the home safer to prevent falls
prevention: There is no proven way to prevent Parkinson's; regular exercise is good for overall health
whenToSeeDoctor: Tremor, stiffness or slowness of movement
Problems with balance or frequent falls
Changes in symptoms or medicine side effects
emergencySigns: A fall with a head injury or inability to get up
Sudden severe confusion or hallucinations
Choking or severe difficulty swallowing

name: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD)
overview: Peripheral arterial disease is a narrowing of the arteries that carry blood to the legs, caused by fatty deposits. It is a sign of a higher risk of heart attack and stroke. Lifestyle changes, exercise and medicines can help.
symptoms: Painful cramping in the hips, thighs or calves when walking, which eases with rest
Hair loss on the legs and feet
Numbness or weakness in the legs
Shiny skin or skin colour changes on the legs
Sores on the feet or legs that do not heal
causes: Build-up of fatty deposits in the leg arteries (atherosclerosis)
Artery damage made worse by smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol
diagnosis: PAD is usually diagnosed by comparing blood pressure in the ankles and arms (ankle-brachial index), sometimes followed by an ultrasound scan.
treatment: Stopping smoking and supervised exercise programmes
Medicines to lower cholesterol, control blood pressure and reduce clotting
Angioplasty or bypass surgery in severe cases
selfCare: Stop smoking
Walk regularly, gradually increasing distance
Look after your feet and check them daily
prevention: Control diabetes, blood pressure and cholesterol
whenToSeeDoctor: Leg pain when walking that goes away with rest
Sores on the legs or feet that do not heal
Cold, numb or discoloured legs or feet
emergencySigns: A suddenly cold, pale, painful, numb leg or foot
Black or dying skin on the toes or foot

name: Pneumonia
overview: Pneumonia is inflammation of the lungs, usually caused by an infection. Many people get better at home in a few weeks, but it can be serious, especially for babies, older adults and people with other health problems.
symptoms: Cough, which may bring up yellow, green or blood-stained mucus
Chest pain when breathing or coughing
Feeling generally unwell, loss of appetite or confusion in older people
causes: Bacterial infection, most commonly pneumococcus
Viral infections such as flu or COVID-19
Less often, fungi or inhaling food or vomit
riskFactors: Long-term lung, heart, kidney or liver conditions
diagnosis: A doctor listens to the chest and checks breathing and oxygen levels; a chest X-ray or blood tests may be used to confirm it.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor for bacterial pneumonia
Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen
Hospital treatment, including oxygen, for severe pneumonia
selfCare: Get plenty of rest
Drink lots of fluids
Do not smoke
Finish any course of antibiotics
prevention: Pneumococcal, flu and COVID-19 vaccines if eligible
whenToSeeDoctor: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Coughing up blood
Chest pain when breathing
Feeling unwell with a cough and high temperature
Breathing problems getting worse
emergencySigns: Severe difficulty breathing or breathing that stops and starts
Lips, tongue or skin turning blue or grey
Sudden confusion or being very drowsy
Coughing up a lot of blood
Chest pain that will not go away

name: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
overview: PCOS is a common condition that affects how the ovaries work. It can cause irregular periods, excess hair growth and difficulty getting pregnant. Symptoms can be managed, and it is linked to a higher risk of type 2 diabetes.
symptoms: Excess hair growth on the face, chest, back or buttocks
Thinning hair or hair loss from the head
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Linked to higher levels of hormones such as testosterone, and insulin resistance
Often runs in families
diagnosis: PCOS is diagnosed from symptoms, blood tests for hormones, and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the ovaries.
treatment: Lifestyle changes such as weight loss if overweight
Hormonal contraceptives to regulate periods
Medicines for excess hair or acne
Fertility treatments if trying to get pregnant
selfCare: Eat a healthy diet
Exercise regularly
Keep to a healthy weight
prevention: Healthy weight and regular activity can reduce symptoms and long-term risks
whenToSeeDoctor: Irregular or missed periods
Difficulty getting pregnant
Excess hair growth or hair loss

name: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
overview: PTSD is a mental health condition that can develop after experiencing or witnessing a frightening or distressing event. People relive the trauma through flashbacks or nightmares and may feel constantly on guard. Effective treatments are available, even years after the event.
symptoms: Reliving the event through flashbacks, nightmares or intrusive images
Feeling on edge, irritable or easily startled
Physical symptoms such as sweating or pain when reminded
causes: Experiencing or witnessing traumatic events such as assault, accidents, abuse, war or disasters
Repeated trauma can lead to complex PTSD
riskFactors: Previous trauma or mental health problems
Lack of support after the event
Jobs with repeated exposure to trauma
diagnosis: A GP or mental health professional diagnoses PTSD by talking about symptoms and how long they have lasted, usually more than a month after the event.
treatment: Trauma-focused talking therapies such as trauma-focused CBT
Eye movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR)
Antidepressant medicines in some cases
selfCare: Talk to people you trust
Keep regular routines for sleep, meals and exercise
Avoid using alcohol or drugs to cope
Join a support group
prevention: Getting support soon after a traumatic event
Seeking help early if symptoms persist
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms lasting more than 4 weeks after a traumatic event
Symptoms affecting daily life or relationships
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Feeling unable to keep yourself or others safe

name: Prostate cancer
overview: Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men. It often grows slowly and may not cause symptoms for many years. Some prostate cancers need treatment, while others can be safely monitored.
symptoms: Often no symptoms in early stages
Needing to pee more often, especially at night
Needing to rush to the toilet
Difficulty starting to pee or a weak flow
Feeling that the bladder has not emptied fully
causes: Changes in prostate cells
Influenced by age, genes and ethnicity
riskFactors: Family history of prostate or breast cancer
Inherited gene changes such as BRCA2
diagnosis: Prostate cancer is investigated with a PSA blood test, an examination, an MRI scan and a biopsy.
treatment: Active surveillance (monitoring) for low-risk cancer
Surgery
Radiotherapy
Hormone therapy and other medicines for advanced cancer
selfCare: Discuss the benefits and risks of PSA testing with a doctor
Stay active and keep to a healthy weight
prevention: There is no proven way to prevent prostate cancer; a healthy lifestyle is recommended
whenToSeeDoctor: Changes in how you pee
Blood in urine or semen
You are at higher risk and want to discuss testing
emergencySigns: Unable to pee
New back pain with numbness or weakness in the legs, or loss of bladder or bowel control

name: Psoriasis
overview: Psoriasis is a long-term skin condition that causes flaky patches of skin covered in scales. It is linked to the immune system and tends to come and go in flare-ups. It is not contagious, and many treatments are available.
symptoms: Raised, flaky patches of skin with silvery-white scales
Patches may look pink or red on lighter skin and purple or dark brown on darker skin
Commonly on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back
Joint pain and swelling in some people (psoriatic arthritis)
causes: An immune system problem that speeds up skin cell production
Genes play a part
Flare-ups triggered by stress, injury to the skin, infections, alcohol, smoking or some medicines
diagnosis: A GP usually diagnoses psoriasis by looking at the skin, scalp and nails.
treatment: Creams and ointments, including emollients, steroid creams and vitamin D-based creams
Light therapy (phototherapy)
Tablets or injections that act on the immune system for more severe psoriasis
selfCare: Use emollients daily
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Keep to a healthy weight
Manage stress
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have psoriasis
Treatment is not working
Painful, swollen or stiff joints
emergencySigns: Widespread red, inflamed skin over most of the body with feeling very unwell or a high temperature
Widespread pus-filled spots with fever

name: Pulmonary embolism
overview: A pulmonary embolism is a blockage of a blood vessel in the lungs, usually by a clot that has travelled from the leg. It can be life-threatening and needs urgent treatment.
symptoms: Chest pain, especially when breathing in
Pain and swelling in a leg (from a DVT)
causes: A blood clot, usually from a deep vein in the leg (DVT), travelling to the lungs
Rarely, a blockage from fat, air or other material entering the bloodstream
riskFactors: Combined hormonal contraception or hormone therapy
diagnosis: A PE is diagnosed in hospital with blood tests and scans such as a CT pulmonary angiogram or a lung scan.
treatment: Anticoagulant medicines
Clot-dissolving medicine or procedures in severe cases
Hospital monitoring
selfCare: Take anticoagulants exactly as prescribed
Stay active as advised during recovery
prevention: Clot prevention measures after surgery or in hospital
whenToSeeDoctor: Breathlessness or chest pain after recent surgery or immobility: seek urgent help
Pain and swelling in one leg, which may be a DVT that could lead to PE
New or worsening symptoms while on treatment
emergencySigns: Sudden breathlessness
Chest pain when breathing in
Coughing up blood
Collapse

name: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)
overview: RSV is a common virus that causes cough and cold symptoms. Most people recover within a few weeks, but it can cause serious breathing problems such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia in babies and older adults. Immunisations are available for some groups.
symptoms: In babies: wheezing, fast breathing and difficulty feeding
causes: Infection with respiratory syncytial virus
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Babies, especially under 6 months or born prematurely
diagnosis: RSV is usually diagnosed from symptoms; a nose or throat swab test may be used in hospital.
treatment: Most people get better at home with rest and fluids
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
Hospital care for breathing or feeding problems
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Wash hands often
Keep away from babies and frail older people while unwell
prevention: RSV vaccine in pregnancy and for older adults where offered
Catch coughs and sneezes in a tissue
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms getting worse
A baby is feeding less or has fewer wet nappies
You have a long-term condition and are worried
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing or pauses in breathing
Lips or skin turning blue or grey
A baby who is floppy or unresponsive
Confusion in older adults

name: Rheumatoid arthritis
overview: Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition where the immune system attacks the joints, causing pain, swelling and stiffness. It usually affects the hands, feet and wrists on both sides of the body. Early treatment helps prevent joint damage.
symptoms: Painful, swollen joints, often the same joints on both sides
Stiffness, especially in the morning, lasting more than 30 minutes
High temperature, sweating and weight loss in some people
Firm lumps under the skin near joints
causes: The immune system attacking the lining of the joints (an autoimmune condition)
A mix of genetic and environmental factors
diagnosis: RA is diagnosed by a GP and rheumatologist using an examination, blood tests for inflammation and antibodies, and X-rays or scans.
treatment: Disease-modifying medicines to slow the disease
Biological and targeted medicines
Painkillers and short-term steroids for flare-ups
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, and sometimes surgery
selfCare: Stay active with regular gentle exercise
Stop smoking
Balance activity with rest
Eat a healthy diet
whenToSeeDoctor: Joint pain, swelling or stiffness lasting more than a few weeks
Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
Flare-ups or side effects if you already have RA
emergencySigns: A single hot, swollen, painful joint with high temperature (possible joint infection)
Fever or signs of serious infection while on immune-suppressing medicine

name: Rosacea
overview: Rosacea is a common long-term skin condition that mainly affects the face, causing redness, flushing and sometimes spots. Symptoms often come and go. Treatment and avoiding triggers can help control it.
symptoms: Redness across the cheeks, nose, chin and forehead (may be harder to see on darker skin)
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Triggers include sunlight, hot or cold weather, alcohol, spicy food, hot drinks, stress and exercise
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses rosacea by looking at the skin and asking about symptoms and triggers.
treatment: Creams and gels prescribed by a doctor
Antibiotic tablets for spots
Laser or light treatment for visible blood vessels
selfCare: Use sunscreen every day
Identify and avoid triggers
Use gentle skincare products
Keep a diary of flare-ups
whenToSeeDoctor: Persistent facial redness or flushing
Spots or skin thickening on the nose
Eye symptoms such as dryness or irritation
emergencySigns: Painful red eye with changes in vision

name: Roseola
overview: Roseola is a common illness in babies and young children. It causes a high temperature followed by a rash. It usually gets better on its own within a week.
symptoms: A sudden high temperature lasting a few days
A rash of small pink or red spots on the chest, tummy and back after the fever goes
causes: Infection with human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) or 7
Spread through saliva and droplets
diagnosis: A doctor diagnoses roseola from the pattern of fever followed by rash.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever
selfCare: Give plenty of fluids
Let your child rest
Keep your child away from others until the fever has gone
whenToSeeDoctor: Your child has a seizure for the first time
Fever lasts more than 5 days
Your child is not feeding or drinking well
Your child is under 3 months with a temperature of 38C or higher
emergencySigns: A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes
Difficulty breathing
A child who is floppy or unresponsive

name: Scabies
overview: Scabies is a common skin condition caused by tiny mites that burrow into the skin. It causes intense itching, especially at night. It spreads easily through close skin contact and is treated with creams or lotions applied to the whole body.
symptoms: Tiny lines (burrows) on the skin, often between the fingers
Rash commonly on the hands, wrists, armpits, waist and genitals
causes: Infestation with Sarcoptes scabiei mites
Spread by prolonged skin-to-skin contact or, less often, shared bedding and clothing
riskFactors: Close contact with an infected person
diagnosis: A pharmacist or GP diagnoses scabies by looking at the rash and burrows.
treatment: Insecticide cream or lotion applied to the whole body, then repeated after a week
Everyone in the household should be treated at the same time
Tablets prescribed by a doctor in some cases
selfCare: Wash bedding, towels and clothes on a hot wash on the day of the first treatment
Seal items that cannot be washed in a bag for 3 days
Avoid close contact until 24 hours after the first treatment
prevention: Treat all close contacts at the same time
Avoid sharing bedding, towels or clothes with someone who has scabies
whenToSeeDoctor: Itching continues more than 4 weeks after treatment
The rash looks infected
You are pregnant or treating a baby under 2 months

name: Scarlet fever
overview: Scarlet fever is a bacterial infection caused by group A streptococcus that mostly affects young children. It causes a rash and flu-like symptoms. It is easily treated with antibiotics.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as high temperature, sore throat and swollen neck glands
A rash appearing 12 to 48 hours later, often starting on the chest and tummy, that feels like sandpaper
On darker skin the rash may be harder to see but still feels rough
A white coating on the tongue that peels, leaving it red and swollen ('strawberry tongue')
causes: Group A streptococcus bacteria
Spread through coughs, sneezes and touching contaminated surfaces
riskFactors: Close contact in schools and nurseries
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses scarlet fever from the symptoms and may take a throat swab.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and discomfort
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids
Eat soft foods if the throat is sore
Use calamine lotion or antihistamines for itching
Stay off school or work until 24 hours after starting antibiotics
prevention: Do not share cutlery, cups or towels
whenToSeeDoctor: You think your child has scarlet fever
Your child is not getting better in a week, or has had chickenpox or measles recently
Your child is dehydrated
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing, with the tummy sucking under the ribs
A child who is floppy, unresponsive or very drowsy
Blue lips or a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Pauses in breathing

name: Schizophrenia
overview: Schizophrenia is a long-term mental health condition that affects how a person thinks, feels and perceives reality. People may experience hallucinations or delusions. With treatment and support, many people manage their symptoms and live well.
symptoms: Hallucinations: hearing or seeing things others do not
Delusions: strong beliefs not shared by others
Losing interest in everyday activities and withdrawing from others
causes: A combination of genetic and environmental factors
Stressful life events or drug use, such as cannabis, can trigger it in people at risk
riskFactors: Heavy cannabis or other drug use, especially in adolescence
diagnosis: Schizophrenia is diagnosed by a psychiatrist after a detailed assessment of symptoms over time, with tests to rule out other causes.
treatment: Antipsychotic medicines
Talking therapies such as CBT for psychosis and family intervention
Support from community mental health teams
Hospital care during severe episodes
selfCare: Take medicine as prescribed
Avoid cannabis and other drugs
Keep regular routines and stay physically active
Stay in contact with your care team
prevention: Avoiding cannabis and drug use may lower risk
Early treatment of psychosis improves outcomes
whenToSeeDoctor: Hearing or seeing things others do not
Unusual beliefs or withdrawal noticed by others
Side effects of medicines
emergencySigns: Thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Risk of harm to self or others
Severe confusion or inability to look after oneself

name: Sciatica
overview: Sciatica is pain caused by irritation or compression of the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back down the legs. It usually gets better within 4 to 6 weeks, but can last longer.
symptoms: Pain, tingling or numbness in the bottom, back of the leg, foot and toes
Pain that is worse when moving, sneezing or coughing
causes: A slipped (herniated) disc pressing on the nerve
Narrowing of the spinal canal (spinal stenosis)
Injury to the spine
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses sciatica from symptoms and an examination; scans are only needed in some cases.
treatment: Staying active and doing exercises
Painkillers
Physiotherapy
Steroid injections or surgery in some cases
selfCare: Keep moving and continue normal activities as much as possible
Use heat packs
Do gentle stretches
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain has not improved after a few weeks
Pain is getting worse or stopping daily activities
Pain in both legs
emergencySigns: Numbness around the genitals or bottom
Loss of bladder or bowel control or unable to pee
Weakness or numbness in both legs that is getting worse

name: Sepsis
overview: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection, where the body's response damages its own tissues and organs. It needs emergency treatment. It can start from any infection, such as a chest or urine infection.
symptoms: Acting confused, slurred speech or not making sense
Blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
A rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it
Difficulty breathing or very fast breathing
Fast heartbeat, high or very low temperature, shivering
causes: The body's overreaction to an infection, often of the lungs, urinary tract, tummy or skin
Infections from wounds, burns or recent surgery, or from medical devices such as catheters
riskFactors: Diabetes or a weakened immune system
Recent surgery, serious illness or wounds
diagnosis: Sepsis is diagnosed in hospital from checks of temperature, heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, plus blood tests.
treatment: Emergency treatment in hospital with antibiotics
Fluids given into a vein and oxygen
Intensive care support if organs are affected
selfCare: Do not wait: call emergency services if you suspect sepsis
Follow rehabilitation advice after recovery, as some people have lasting effects
prevention: Keep up to date with vaccinations
whenToSeeDoctor: Feeling very unwell with an infection that is not improving or is getting worse
A child or adult with an infection who seems much more unwell than expected
emergencySigns: Confusion, slurred speech or not making sense
Blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
Rash that does not fade under a glass
Difficulty breathing or very fast breathing
Not passing urine all day

name: Shingles
overview: Shingles is a painful rash caused by the chickenpox virus becoming active again later in life. It usually affects one side of the body and gets better in about 2 to 4 weeks. Early treatment can help, and a vaccine is offered to some age groups.
symptoms: Tingling or burning feeling in an area of skin before the rash appears
A painful rash of blisters on one side of the body, often the chest or tummy
Rash may also appear on the face, eyes or ears
causes: Reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus that stays dormant in the nerves after chickenpox
Reactivation is more likely when the immune system is weaker, such as with age, illness or some medicines
riskFactors: Having had chickenpox in the past
diagnosis: A doctor usually diagnoses shingles from the appearance and pattern of the rash.
treatment: Antiviral medicine, ideally started within 3 days of the rash appearing
Painkillers for pain
Stronger pain treatment if nerve pain continues after the rash heals
selfCare: Keep the rash clean and dry
Wear loose-fitting clothes
Use a cool compress
Avoid contact with pregnant people, babies and people with weak immunity until blisters have scabbed
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have shingles, especially within 3 days of the rash
You are pregnant or have a weakened immune system
Pain continues after the rash has cleared
emergencySigns: Rash near the eye with eye pain, redness or changes in vision
Rash spreading over a large area of the body with feeling very unwell
Weakness of the face, confusion or severe headache

name: Sickle cell disease
overview: Sickle cell disease is an inherited condition that affects red blood cells, making them an unusual shape. It can cause painful episodes, anaemia and a higher risk of infections. Treatment and care can help people live well.
symptoms: Tiredness and shortness of breath from anaemia
Yellowing of the skin or eyes
causes: An inherited change in the gene for haemoglobin
A child must inherit the gene from both parents to have the disease
riskFactors: Both parents carrying the sickle cell gene
Family origins in Africa, the Caribbean, the Middle East, India or the Mediterranean
diagnosis: Sickle cell disease is diagnosed with a blood test; many countries screen newborns and offer screening in pregnancy.

Medicines to reduce crises
Antibiotics and vaccines to prevent infections
Blood transfusions, and stem cell or gene therapies for some people
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids
Avoid extreme temperatures
Avoid overexertion
Keep up with vaccines and prescribed medicines
prevention: Carrier screening and genetic counselling for couples who may both carry the gene
whenToSeeDoctor: Pain not controlled at home
Signs of infection
Increasing tiredness or paleness
emergencySigns: High temperature
Chest pain or difficulty breathing
Severe pain not relieved by usual medicine
Sudden weakness, confusion or problems speaking
A painful erection lasting more than 2 hours

name: Sinusitis
overview: Sinusitis is swelling of the sinuses, the air-filled spaces behind the face, usually after a cold. Most cases clear up on their own within 2 to 3 weeks. It can sometimes last longer and become chronic.
symptoms: Pain, swelling and tenderness around the cheeks, eyes or forehead
Thick green or yellow nasal discharge
causes: A cold or flu virus spreading to the sinuses
Less often, a bacterial infection
Allergies such as hay fever
Nasal polyps
diagnosis: A doctor usually diagnoses sinusitis from the symptoms and an examination; scans or referral are only needed for long-lasting or recurrent cases.
treatment: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain
Decongestant nasal sprays for short-term use
Steroid nasal sprays prescribed by a doctor for longer-lasting symptoms
Antibiotics only if a bacterial infection is likely

Hold a warm compress over the face
Rinse the nose with a salt-water solution
Avoid smoking
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms are severe
Symptoms do not improve after 10 days or keep coming back
Symptoms get worse after starting to improve
emergencySigns: Swelling or redness around the eyes
Changes in vision such as double vision
Severe headache with a stiff neck or confusion

name: Slapped cheek syndrome
overview: Slapped cheek syndrome is a common viral infection in children that causes a bright red rash on the cheeks. It is usually mild and gets better on its own within 3 weeks. It can occasionally be more serious for pregnant people and people with some blood disorders.
symptoms: Mild cold-like symptoms such as high temperature, runny nose and sore throat
A bright red rash on both cheeks (may be less noticeable on darker skin)
A few days later, a spotty rash on the chest, arms and legs
causes: Infection with parvovirus B19
Spread through coughs and sneezes
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses slapped cheek syndrome from the typical rash; a blood test may be done in pregnancy.
treatment: No specific treatment; it gets better on its own
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and joint pain
Antihistamines or emollients for itching
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Children can usually go to school once the rash appears, as they are no longer infectious
prevention: Pregnant people in contact with it should speak to a doctor
whenToSeeDoctor: You are pregnant and have been in contact with slapped cheek syndrome or have a rash
You have a blood disorder such as sickle cell disease or a weakened immune system
Symptoms are severe or not improving

A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it

name: Stomach ulcer
overview: Stomach ulcers are open sores in the lining of the stomach or the first part of the small intestine. They are usually caused by H. pylori infection or anti-inflammatory painkillers, and are usually treatable.
symptoms: Burning or gnawing pain in the centre of the tummy
Some people have no symptoms until bleeding occurs

Taking anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen or aspirin, especially long term

treatment: Acid-reducing medicines prescribed by a doctor
Antibiotics to clear H. pylori infection
Stopping or changing anti-inflammatory painkillers where possible
selfCare: Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers unless advised
Stop smoking
Cut down on alcohol
prevention: Use anti-inflammatory painkillers only as needed and with advice
whenToSeeDoctor: Ongoing tummy pain or indigestion
Symptoms that keep coming back
You take anti-inflammatory painkillers regularly and have tummy pain
emergencySigns: Vomiting blood or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Black, sticky, tarry poo
Sudden, sharp tummy pain that gets steadily worse

name: Strep throat
overview: Strep throat is a throat infection caused by group A streptococcus bacteria. It is most common in children and is treated with antibiotics. Most sore throats are caused by viruses rather than strep.
symptoms: Red, swollen tonsils, sometimes with white patches
Swollen, tender glands in the neck
causes: Infection with group A streptococcus bacteria
Spread by droplets from coughs, sneezes or close contact
riskFactors: Close contact with someone who has strep
Crowded settings such as schools and nurseries
diagnosis: A doctor examines the throat and may take a throat swab for a rapid strep test or a laboratory culture.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain and fever
Finish the full antibiotic course even when feeling better
selfCare: Drink plenty of fluids
Eat soft, cool foods
Gargle with warm salty water (adults and older children)
Rest

Stay off school or work until at least 24 hours after starting antibiotics, or as advised
whenToSeeDoctor: Sore throat with high temperature and no cough

name: Stroke
overview: A stroke is a medical emergency where the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off, by a clot or by bleeding. The faster treatment starts, the less damage there is. Weakness or numbness in one arm or leg
Sudden loss of vision, dizziness or loss of balance

Medicines to prevent further strokes
