Take part in rehabilitation and take prevention medicines as prescribed

name: Syphilis
overview: Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection. It often starts with a painless sore and can be easily missed. It is cured with antibiotics, but without treatment it can cause serious problems years later.

From mother to baby during pregnancy
riskFactors: Men who have sex with men

Tell recent sexual partners
whenToSeeDoctor: A sore or rash on the genitals, anus or mouth
A partner has syphilis
You are pregnant and have not been screened

Severe headache, confusion or weakness

name: Tension-type headache
overview: Tension-type headaches are the most common kind of headache. They feel like a constant ache or pressure around the head, like a tight band. They are usually not serious and can be eased with simple painkillers and lifestyle changes.

A feeling of tightness or pressure around the forehead
Tight or tender neck and shoulder muscles
Can usually carry on with normal activities

Poor posture
Lack of sleep
Skipping meals or not drinking enough fluids
Eye strain

Physiotherapy or relaxation techniques
selfCare: Regular exercise
Relaxation and stress management
Drink enough water and eat regularly
Improve posture and take screen breaks
whenToSeeDoctor: Headaches several times a week or getting worse

Headaches with other symptoms such as numbness or weakness
emergencySigns: Sudden, severe headache

name: Threadworms
overview: Threadworms are tiny worms in poo. They are common in children and spread easily. They can be treated with medicine from a pharmacy and strict hygiene.

Strict hygiene measures for 2 weeks

Bath or shower every morning
Wash bedding, towels and soft toys
Keep nails short and discourage scratching
whenToSeeDoctor: Your child is under 2
You are pregnant or breastfeeding
Treatment has not worked

name: Tinnitus
overview: Tinnitus is hearing noises such as ringing or buzzing that are not caused by an outside source. It is common and often linked to hearing loss. It may improve over time, and there are ways to manage it.
symptoms: Ringing, buzzing, humming, whooshing or hissing sounds
Sounds that come and go or are constant
causes: Hearing loss from ageing or loud noise
Earwax build-up
Ear infections
Ménière's disease
Anxiety or stress
Some medicines

Hearing aids if hearing loss is present
Sound therapy
Talking therapies such as CBT

Avoid very quiet environments

whenToSeeDoctor: Tinnitus that does not go away or is getting worse

name: Tonsillitis
overview: Tonsillitis is an infection of the tonsils at the back of the throat. It is common in children but can affect anyone, and usually gets better on its own within about a week.
symptoms: Swollen, red tonsils, sometimes with white pus-filled spots
causes: Usually a viral infection
Sometimes a bacterial infection such as group A strep
riskFactors: Close contact with people who have throat infections
diagnosis: A GP looks at the throat and asks about symptoms; a throat swab is sometimes taken to check for bacteria.
treatment: Rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen
Antibiotics if a bacterial infection is likely
Surgery to remove the tonsils is only considered for frequent, severe tonsillitis
selfCare: Get plenty of rest
Drink cool drinks
Eat soft foods
Gargle with warm salty water (not for children)
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms do not improve after 4 days
Severe pain making it hard to eat or drink
Very high temperature
Frequent episodes of tonsillitis
emergencySigns: Difficulty breathing
Drooling or unable to swallow
Making a high-pitched sound when breathing
Symptoms getting rapidly worse

name: Tuberculosis (TB)
overview: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs but can affect other parts of the body. It spreads through the air when someone with active TB in the lungs coughs. It is curable with a long course of antibiotics taken exactly as prescribed.
symptoms: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks, which may bring up mucus or blood
Weight loss and loss of appetite
Swellings in the neck or other glands
causes: Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria
Breathing in bacteria from the coughs or sneezes of someone with active lung TB, usually after prolonged close contact
riskFactors: Close contact with someone with active TB
Living in or travelling to areas where TB is common
HIV or another cause of a weakened immune system
diagnosis: Doctors use a chest X-ray, tests on samples of mucus, and skin or blood tests to look for TB infection.
treatment: A combination of antibiotics taken for several months
Taking every dose for the full course to cure TB and prevent drug resistance
Treatment of latent TB to stop it becoming active in some people
selfCare: Take medicines exactly as prescribed
Cover your mouth when coughing and ventilate rooms while infectious
Eat well and avoid alcohol and smoking
prevention: BCG vaccine for people at higher risk, as offered
Screening and treatment of close contacts
Early diagnosis and full treatment of people with TB
whenToSeeDoctor: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Unexplained weight loss, fever or night sweats
You have been in close contact with someone with TB
emergencySigns: Coughing up a lot of blood
Severe difficulty breathing
Severe headache with a stiff neck or confusion

name: Type 1 diabetes
overview: Type 1 diabetes is a lifelong condition where the immune system destroys the cells that make insulin, so blood sugar becomes too high. It often starts in childhood or young adulthood but can begin at any age. It is managed with insulin and regular glucose monitoring.
symptoms: Peeing more than usual, especially at night
causes: The immune system attacking the insulin-producing cells in the pancreas
Genetic and possibly environmental triggers, which are not fully understood
diagnosis: Type 1 diabetes is diagnosed with blood tests for sugar levels, along with tests for ketones and sometimes antibodies; it needs urgent same-day assessment.
treatment: Insulin by injection or pump
Regular blood glucose checks or continuous glucose monitoring
Education on carbohydrate counting and adjusting insulin
Regular checks for complications affecting eyes, feet and kidneys
selfCare: Check blood sugar regularly
Learn to recognise and treat low blood sugar (hypos)
Eat a healthy diet and stay active
Attend annual reviews including eye screening
prevention: There is currently no known way to prevent type 1 diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms of diabetes such as thirst, peeing a lot or weight loss (seek same-day advice)
Frequent hypos or high blood sugar readings
Problems with feet, eyes or injection sites
emergencySigns: Vomiting, tummy pain, fast breathing or a fruity smell on the breath (possible diabetic ketoacidosis)
Confusion, drowsiness or unconsciousness
A severe hypo that does not respond to treatment

name: Type 2 diabetes
overview: Type 2 diabetes is a common condition where the body does not make enough insulin or the insulin does not work properly, so blood sugar becomes too high. It develops gradually and often has no symptoms at first. It can be managed with lifestyle changes and medicines, and is linked to being overweight.
symptoms: Peeing more than usual, especially at night
Cuts or wounds that heal slowly, blurred vision, or itching around the genitals
causes: The body becoming resistant to insulin or not making enough of it
Strongly linked to excess weight, inactivity and genes
riskFactors: Age over 40 (over 25 for people of South Asian, Chinese, African-Caribbean or Black African descent)
diagnosis: Type 2 diabetes is diagnosed with a blood test, usually an HbA1c test that shows average blood sugar over the past few months.
treatment: Healthy diet, weight loss and exercise
Medicines to lower blood sugar, prescribed by a doctor
Insulin in some people
Regular checks of eyes, feet, kidneys, blood pressure and cholesterol
selfCare: Eat a healthy, balanced diet
Be physically active
Lose weight if overweight
Stop smoking and limit alcohol
Check your feet daily
prevention: Eat a diet low in sugar and processed foods and high in fibre
Join a diabetes prevention programme if offered
whenToSeeDoctor: Symptoms of diabetes
You are at high risk and have not been tested
Foot problems such as cuts or sores that are not healing
emergencySigns: Confusion, extreme drowsiness or unconsciousness
Very high blood sugar with vomiting, severe thirst and dehydration
A severe hypo (low blood sugar) on insulin or certain tablets that does not respond to treatment

name: Ulcerative colitis
overview: Ulcerative colitis is a long-term condition where the colon and rectum become inflamed and develop ulcers. It is a type of inflammatory bowel disease. Symptoms come and go, and treatment helps control flare-ups and keep the condition in remission.
symptoms: Diarrhoea, often with blood, mucus or pus
Needing to poo urgently and often
causes: The exact cause is unknown
Thought to be an immune system problem combined with genes and environment
riskFactors: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease
diagnosis: It is diagnosed with blood and stool tests and a colonoscopy or sigmoidoscopy with biopsies.
treatment: Anti-inflammatory medicines
Steroids for flare-ups
Immunosuppressants and biological medicines
Surgery to remove the colon in severe cases
selfCare: Keep a food and symptom diary
Drink enough fluids during flare-ups
Take medicines as prescribed even when well
Join a support group
prevention: Take maintenance treatment as prescribed to reduce flare-ups
whenToSeeDoctor: Blood in your poo or diarrhoea for more than 7 days
Signs of a flare-up if you already have UC
emergencySigns: Passing a lot of blood
Severe tummy pain or swelling
Fever with fast heartbeat and feeling very unwell
More than 6 bloody poos a day

name: Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism)
overview: An underactive thyroid means the thyroid gland does not make enough thyroid hormone. Symptoms develop slowly and can be mistaken for other things. It is common, especially in women, and is treated with daily hormone replacement tablets.
symptoms: Dry skin, brittle hair and muscle aches
causes: The immune system attacking the thyroid (Hashimoto's thyroiditis)
Previous thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine treatment
Some medicines
Iodine deficiency in some parts of the world
riskFactors: Other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes
diagnosis: An underactive thyroid is diagnosed with a blood test measuring thyroid hormone levels (TSH and T4).
treatment: Daily thyroid hormone replacement tablets
Regular blood tests to check the dose
selfCare: Take tablets as advised, usually at the same time each day
Attend regular blood tests
Tell your doctor if you become pregnant
prevention: There is usually no way to prevent it, but early testing helps
whenToSeeDoctor: Ongoing tiredness, weight gain or feeling cold
Symptoms do not improve on treatment
You are pregnant or planning pregnancy and have a thyroid condition
emergencySigns: Extreme drowsiness, confusion or very low body temperature (rare but serious)

name: Urinary incontinence
overview: Urinary incontinence means accidentally passing urine. It is common, especially in women and older people, and is often treatable. Many people feel embarrassed, but doctors can help.
symptoms: Leaking urine when coughing, sneezing, laughing or exercising (stress incontinence)
A sudden, intense urge to pee, with leaking before reaching the toilet (urge incontinence)
Needing to pee often, including at night
causes: Weakened pelvic floor muscles, often after pregnancy and childbirth
Overactive bladder muscles
Menopause
An enlarged prostate in men
Some medicines or neurological conditions
diagnosis: A GP asks about symptoms, may examine you, and may test your urine or ask you to keep a bladder diary.
treatment: Pelvic floor muscle exercises
Bladder training
Medicines for urge incontinence
Surgery or procedures in some cases
selfCare: Do pelvic floor exercises daily
Cut down on caffeine and alcohol
Keep to a healthy weight
Avoid constipation
whenToSeeDoctor: Any leaking of urine that affects your life
Incontinence starting suddenly
Blood in urine or pain when peeing
emergencySigns: Sudden loss of bladder control with numbness around the bottom or weakness in the legs
Unable to pee at all with tummy pain

name: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
overview: Urinary tract infections affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys. They are very common, especially in women. Mild bladder infections may get better on their own, but many are treated with antibiotics.
symptoms: Needing to pee more often or more urgently
Confusion or agitation in older people
causes: Bacteria, usually from the bowel, getting into the urethra and bladder
Things that make it easier for bacteria to enter or stay in the bladder, such as sex, catheters, or not emptying the bladder fully
riskFactors: Conditions that block the flow of urine, such as kidney stones or an enlarged prostate
diagnosis: A GP or pharmacist usually diagnoses a UTI from symptoms; a urine test may be used, especially for men, children, pregnant people or repeated infections.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor, nurse or pharmacist
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain
selfCare: Drink plenty of water to pee regularly
Rest
Avoid sex until you feel better
prevention: Wipe from front to back after using the toilet
Pee as soon as possible after sex
Drink enough fluids so urine is pale
whenToSeeDoctor: You are a man, pregnant, or have a child with symptoms
Symptoms are not improving or keep coming back
Blood in your urine
Symptoms after surgery or with a catheter
emergencySigns: High temperature with shivering and pain in the back or side (possible kidney infection)
Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking
Not passing any urine all day
Very fast breathing or heartbeat

name: Vaginal thrush
overview: Vaginal thrush is a common yeast infection. It is not usually serious, is not a sexually transmitted infection, and can be treated with pharmacy medicines.
symptoms: White vaginal discharge, often like cottage cheese, which does not usually smell
Itching and irritation around the vagina
Soreness and stinging during sex or when peeing
causes: Overgrowth of Candida yeast, which normally lives harmlessly in the body
Changes that upset the natural balance in the vagina, such as antibiotics, hormone changes or high blood sugar
diagnosis: Thrush is often recognised from symptoms; a GP or sexual health clinic may take a swab if it keeps coming back or the diagnosis is unclear.
treatment: Antifungal pessaries, creams or tablets from a pharmacy or prescribed by a doctor
Longer treatment for recurring thrush
selfCare: Use water and emollient instead of soap to wash
Dry properly after washing
Wear cotton underwear
Avoid perfumed products and douching
prevention: Control blood sugar if you have diabetes
whenToSeeDoctor: It is your first time having symptoms
You are pregnant or under 16
Treatment has not worked or thrush keeps coming back
Unusual discharge, smell, bleeding or sores

name: Varicose veins
overview: Varicose veins are swollen, twisted veins, usually in the legs, caused by weak valves in the veins. They are common and often harmless, though they can ache or itch. Treatment is usually only needed if they cause problems.
symptoms: Blue or dark purple, bulging, twisted veins
Burning or throbbing in the legs
Dry, itchy skin over the vein
causes: Weak or damaged valves inside the veins that let blood flow backwards and collect
Increased pressure in the leg veins, for example from pregnancy, overweight or long periods of standing
riskFactors: Jobs involving long periods of standing
diagnosis: A GP diagnoses varicose veins by looking at the legs; an ultrasound scan may be done if treatment is considered.
treatment: Compression stockings
Procedures such as heat or laser treatment to seal veins
Injections to close veins (sclerotherapy)
Surgery to remove veins in some cases
selfCare: Avoid standing still for long periods
Raise the legs when resting
Exercise regularly
Keep to a healthy weight
prevention: Avoid standing or sitting for long periods without moving
whenToSeeDoctor: Veins are painful or causing discomfort
Skin over the veins is changing colour, sore or itchy
Veins become hot, red and painful (possible inflammation)
emergencySigns: A vein that is bleeding heavily and does not stop with pressure
Sudden leg swelling and pain with breathlessness or chest pain

name: Whooping cough
overview: Whooping cough is a bacterial infection of the lungs and breathing tubes that causes long bouts of coughing. It can be very serious for young babies. Vaccination in pregnancy and childhood helps protect babies.
symptoms: Cold-like symptoms at first, such as runny nose and sore throat
Coughing bouts lasting a few minutes, worse at night
A 'whoop' sound when breathing in between coughs
Bringing up thick mucus or vomiting after coughing
Babies may not whoop but may stop breathing briefly or turn blue
causes: Bordetella pertussis bacteria
Spread through coughs and sneezes
riskFactors: Babies too young to be fully vaccinated
Close contact with someone with whooping cough
diagnosis: A doctor may suspect it from the cough and confirm it with a nose or throat swab or a blood test.
treatment: Antibiotics if diagnosed early, to reduce spread
Hospital treatment for babies with severe whooping cough
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Stay away from nursery, school or work until 48 hours after starting antibiotics, or 3 weeks after coughing started
Keep away from babies
prevention: Whooping cough vaccine in pregnancy to protect newborns
whenToSeeDoctor: A baby under 6 months has symptoms
Coughing bouts that are getting worse
You are pregnant and have been in contact with whooping cough
A cough that lasts for weeks
emergencySigns: Lips, tongue or skin turning blue or grey
Pauses in breathing or difficulty breathing
Seizures
A baby who is floppy or unresponsive
